value.dimension: Anthropic guidance on agentic coding & multi-agent systems

findings.claim: Compose the funnel from Anthropic's five workflow primitives and add each stage only when it demonstrably improves outcomes; put programmatic 'gates' between stages and give every agent loop a stopping condition.
findings.evidence: Building effective agents defines workflows (predefined code paths) vs agents, and lists prompt chaining ('you can add programmatic checks (see "gate" in the diagram below) on any intermediate steps'), routing, parallelization (sectioning + voting, e.g. 'Reviewing code for vulnerabilities with multiple prompts'), orchestrator-workers ('well-suited for complex tasks where you can't predict the subtasks needed'), evaluator-optimizer ('particularly effective when we have clear evaluation criteria'). It says to add complexity 'only when it demonstrably improves outcomes', that 'The autonomous nature of agents means higher costs, and the potential for compounding errors', and to implement 'stopping conditions (such as a maximum number of iterations)'.
findings.implication: The funnel maps 1:1: routing at intake (triage by complexity), orchestrator-workers for decomposition/distribution, a gate for the hypothesis check, parallel voting for reviewers, evaluator-optimizer for the send-back loop. Each loop needs a max-iteration cap; simple tasks must be routed around the heavy stages or the funnel will slow work instead of accelerating it.

findings.claim: Every delegation must carry an objective, an output format, allowed tools/sources, and explicit task boundaries, plus an effort budget scaled to task complexity; vague delegations cause duplicated and missing work.
findings.evidence: Multi-agent research post: early agents were 'spawning 50 subagents for simple queries'; with vague prompts 'one subagent explored the 2021 automotive chip crisis while 2 others duplicated work'. Fix: each subagent needs 'an objective, an output format, guidance on the tools and sources to use, and clear task boundaries'. Effort rules embedded in the prompt: 'Simple fact-finding requires just 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls, direct comparisons might need 2-4 subagents with 10-15 calls each'.
findings.implication: The 'distribution' stage should emit a machine-readable delegation contract per unit (objective, JSON output schema, tool allowlist, file ownership, budget). Encode effort-scaling rules in the orchestrator prompt so trivial tasks never fan out.

findings.claim: Multi-agent systems cost ~15x a chat's tokens and pay off mainly for breadth-heavy, parallelizable, read-dominant work; coding has fewer truly parallel parts, so parallelize exploration and review but keep writes few and disjoint.
findings.evidence: Post reports the multi-agent system 'outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2%' on a research eval but 'token usage by itself explains 80% of the variance' and multi-agent uses 'about 15x more tokens than chats'. The post's suitability section (paraphrased; not in my extracted quotes) says tasks needing shared context or many inter-dependencies are a poor fit and most coding tasks have fewer parallelizable pieces than research. Claude Code docs enforce disjoint writes via worktrees and 'each teammate owns a different set of files'.
findings.implication: Fan out for exploration, hypothesis generation, and review; serialize or partition implementation by file ownership (worktrees). Budget the funnel explicitly and route small tasks to a lightweight path so the average task is faster, not slower.

findings.claim: Separate the evaluator from the generator and tune it to be skeptical; negotiate a 'sprint contract' defining 'done' and how it will be verified BEFORE any code is written; have the evaluator exercise the product as a user would.
findings.evidence: Harness-design post: 'when asked to evaluate work they've produced, agents tend to respond by confidently praising the work—even when, to a human observer, the quality is obviously mediocre'; 'tuning a standalone evaluator to be skeptical turns out to be far more tractable'. 'the generator and evaluator negotiated a sprint contract: agreeing on what "done" looked like for that chunk of work before any code was written.' Evaluator 'used the Playwright MCP to click through the running application the way a user would'. Costs: solo agent 20 min/$9 (broken) vs harness 6 hr/$200 (working); v2 DAW build $124.70 with ~$3 QA rounds.
findings.implication: This is the Anthropic-backed form of the user's 'hypothesis check before implementation': a contract artifact (what + verification method) vetted by a separate agent. The same contract later becomes the acceptance criteria that independent and outside reviewers grade against.

findings.claim: Independent review must run in a fresh context that sees only the diff and the criteria (not the reasoning), and reviewers must be told to report only correctness/requirement gaps because a gap-hunting reviewer always finds something.
findings.evidence: Best practices: 'A reviewer running in a fresh subagent context sees only the diff and the criteria you give it, not the reasoning that produced the change, so it evaluates the result on its own terms.' Template: 'review the rate limiter diff against PLAN.md. Check that every requirement is implemented, the listed edge cases have tests, and nothing outside the task's scope changed. Report gaps, not style preferences.' Caveat: 'A reviewer prompted to find gaps will usually report some, even when the work is sound... Chasing every finding leads to over-engineering'. Also: 'A fresh context improves code review since Claude won't be biased toward code it just wrote.'
findings.implication: Implement the 'send-back' reviewer as a .claude/agents subagent (or context: fork skill) that receives diff + contract only, returns structured findings limited to correctness, with a nit cap and a re-review rule ('second round: Important findings only') so the loop converges instead of gold-plating.

findings.claim: Every stage must end with a check that produces a pass/fail signal the agent can read (tests, build exit code, fixture diff, screenshot compare); gate the stop with /goal, a Stop hook, or a verification subagent, and require evidence rather than claims of success.
findings.evidence: 'Claude stops when the work looks done. Without a check it can run, "looks done" is the only signal available, and you become the verification loop.' Ladder: in-prompt check; '/goal condition. A separate evaluator re-checks it after every turn'; 'a Stop hook runs your check as a script and blocks the turn from ending until it passes'; 'a verification subagent... has a fresh model try to refute the result, so the agent doing the work isn't the one grading it.' 'Have Claude show evidence rather than asserting success'. /goal doc: the evaluator 'doesn't run commands or read files independently, so write the condition as something Claude's own output can demonstrate'.
findings.implication: The contract from the hypothesis stage must name a runnable check; execution is gated by a deterministic Stop hook (or /goal) on that check; reviewers get the evidence (test output, screenshots) as part of the artifact bundle.

findings.claim: Use hooks, not CLAUDE.md text, for anything that must hold every time: hooks are deterministic (exit 2 blocks), CLAUDE.md is advisory; Stop hooks are capped at 8 consecutive blocks and must honor stop_hook_active.
findings.evidence: 'Unlike CLAUDE.md instructions which are advisory, hooks are deterministic and guarantee the action happens.' Features overview: 'An instruction like "never edit .env" in CLAUDE.md or a skill is a request, not a guarantee. A PreToolUse hook that blocks the edit is enforcement.' Hooks reference: 'Exit 2 means a blocking error. On events that can block, exit 2 blocks whether or not you print JSON.' Guide: 'Claude Code overrides a Stop hook after it blocks eight times in a row without progress'; prompt hooks return {ok:false, reason} and for Stop 'the reason is fed back to Claude so it keeps working, unless the response also sets "impossible": true'; agent hooks can 'Verify that all unit tests pass'. Hooks also run inside subagents with agent_id/agent_type; TaskCompleted/TeammateIdle can 'Exit with code 2 to prevent completion and send feedback'.
findings.implication: Implement funnel gates as hooks: PostToolUse lint/typecheck on Edit|Write, PreToolUse blocks on protected paths and on editing tests, Stop/SubagentStop gates on the contract check, TaskCompleted gate that refuses completion without evidence. Keep the block cap in mind so gates converge.

findings.claim: Plan before coding for multi-file or unfamiliar changes, but skip planning when the diff fits in one sentence; for large features, have Claude interview you, write SPEC.md, then execute in a fresh session.
findings.evidence: 'Letting Claude jump straight to coding can produce code that solves the wrong problem.' 'If you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan.' Interview prompt: 'Interview me in detail using the AskUserQuestion tool... Keep interviewing until we've covered everything, then write a complete spec to SPEC.md.' 'Once the spec is complete, start a fresh session to execute it.' Good specs 'name the files and interfaces involved, state what is out of scope, and end with an end-to-end verification step'. Plan mode 'reads files, runs shell commands to explore, and writes a plan, but does not edit your source'.
findings.implication: The wide intake stage is an interview that produces SPEC.md; a routing rule decides between the light path (direct fix + test) and the full funnel; execution always starts from a clean context reading the spec, not from the planning transcript.

findings.claim: Context is the binding constraint: performance degrades as context fills ('context rot'); reset after two failed corrections; keep research in subagents; keep CLAUDE.md under ~200 lines and move scoped guidance to .claude/rules with paths and procedures to skills.
findings.evidence: Best practices: 'Claude's context window fills up fast, and performance degrades as it fills'; 'If you've corrected Claude more than twice on the same issue in one session... Run /clear'; named failure patterns (kitchen sink session, over-specified CLAUDE.md, infinite exploration). Context-engineering post: 'context rot'; sub-agents return 'only a condensed, distilled summary'; 'overly aggressive compaction can result in the loss of subtle but critical context'. Memory docs: 'target under 200 lines per CLAUDE.md file'; path-scoped rules 'only load into context when Claude works with matching files'; 'if two rules contradict each other, Claude may pick one arbitrarily'.
findings.implication: Design every funnel stage to start from a fresh context plus on-disk artifacts (spec, contract, features.json, progress file) rather than a shared transcript; the 'straight line of errors' the user describes is largely context pollution, and stage boundaries are where you clear it.

findings.claim: For long-running work use an initializer that writes a JSON feature list (all passes:false), init.sh, a progress file and a baseline commit; work one feature at a time; forbid editing tests; start every session with a fixed ritual and an end-to-end smoke test; commit per feature as a checkpoint.
findings.evidence: Effective harnesses post: feature entries like {"description": "New chat button creates a fresh conversation", "passes": false}; 'It is unacceptable to remove or edit tests because this could lead to missing or buggy functionality'; JSON because 'the model is less likely to inappropriately change or overwrite JSON files compared to Markdown'; one feature at a time 'turned out to be critical to addressing the agent's tendency to do too much at once'; agents marked features done without testing, fixed by 'do all testing as a human user would'. Session start: pwd, git log + progress file, pick failing feature, run init.sh, 'Execute basic end-to-end verification'. Platform docs add: prefer 'a brand new context window rather than using compaction' since models are 'extremely effective at discovering state from the local filesystem'.
findings.implication: The decomposition stage should produce features.json as the funnel's ledger; execution workers claim one feature, must flip passes only with evidence, and every fresh worker/reviewer bootstraps from disk state, making the funnel resumable and tool-agnostic.

findings.claim: Grade the end state, not the path; write acceptance criteria so that two experts would give the same pass/fail; measure consistency with pass^k; build the funnel's own eval from 20-50 real past failures and read the transcripts.
findings.evidence: Demystifying evals: 'It's often better to grade what the agent produced, not the path it took'; 'A good task is one where two domain experts would independently reach the same pass/fail verdict'; 'By k=10... pass@k approaches 100% while pass^k falls to 0%'; 'Begin with 20-50 simple tasks drawn from real failures'; 'You won't know if your graders are working well unless you read the transcripts'; 'Make your graders resistant to bypasses or hacks'; grading bugs took Opus 4.5 on CORE-Bench from 42% to 95%. Multi-agent post: LLM judge rubric (accuracy, citations, completeness, source quality, efficiency) with 'evaluate whether it achieved the correct final state'.
findings.implication: The outside 'verdict' reviewers should grade outcomes against unambiguous criteria from the contract, not process; the funnel itself should be regression-tested on a small suite of the user's real past failures, tracking pass^k since 'error-free' means consistency.

findings.claim: Production-grade code review = many parallel reviewers each with one narrow lens -> a verification pass that reproduces/refutes each candidate finding -> dedupe and rank by severity; Anthropic's internal data shows <1% findings marked incorrect and substantive-comment rate rising from 16% to 54%.
findings.evidence: Code Review blog: 'The agents look for bugs in parallel, verify bugs to filter out false positives, and rank bugs by severity'; 'Reviews scale with the PR'; large PRs '84% get findings, averaging 7.5 issues', small PRs 31%/0.5; 'less than 1% of findings are marked incorrect'; $15-25 and ~20 min per PR. Docs: 'Each agent looks for a different class of issue, then a verification step checks candidates against actual code behavior'; check run 'never blocks merging'; REVIEW.md knobs: 'behavior claims need a file:line citation in the source, not an inference from naming', 'report at most five nits', 'after the first review, suppress new nits and post Important findings only'. Ultrareview: 'every reported finding is independently reproduced and verified'.
findings.implication: The 'outside reviewers' stage should be a lens-per-agent fan-out (logic, boundaries, API misuse, security, conventions) followed by refuter agents and a ranker; findings need file:line evidence and severity; note <1% is precision only, so this layer reduces but cannot guarantee zero misses.

findings.claim: Codify the orchestration as a dynamic workflow script: the script (not the model) holds the plan and intermediate results, can make independent agents adversarially cross-check findings, enforces JSON output schemas with validation retries, and is resumable and deterministic; stages needing human sign-off must be separate workflows.
findings.evidence: Workflows docs: 'A workflow script holds the loop, the branching, and the intermediate results itself, so Claude's context holds only the final answer'; 'it can have independent agents adversarially review each other's findings before they're reported, or draft a plan from several angles'; schema option: 'If the subagent's output still fails validation after five attempts, the call fails'; 'Date.now(), Math.random()... throw inside the script' for replay; 'No mid-run user input... For sign-off between stages, run each stage as its own workflow'; limits 16 concurrent agents, 1,000 per run; /deep-research 'votes on each claim... claims that didn't survive cross-checking filtered out'.
findings.implication: Implement the funnel as saved .claude/workflows scripts (one per stage or stage-group), with agent() schemas as the typed hand-offs between zones of responsibility; this gives reproducibility, resumability, and a reviewable orchestration, satisfying 'universal' and 'reusable'.

findings.claim: Define funnel roles as narrow subagents with tool allowlists, per-role models, maxTurns, spawn restrictions, and short descriptions; subagents see no conversation history and return only a summary, and are the wrong tool for iterative back-and-forth.
findings.evidence: Sub-agents docs: subagent returns 'only the summary'; frontmatter supports tools/disallowedTools, model, effort, maxTurns, permissionMode, skills, memory, isolation: worktree, hooks; 'Claude uses each subagent's description to decide when to delegate'; combined descriptions over 15,000 tokens warn; 'tools: Agent(worker, researcher)' restricts what a coordinator can spawn; limits: 20 concurrent, depth 3; don't use for 'Iterative refinement', 'Shared context', 'Quick changes'. Platform docs: 'Claude Opus 4.6 has a strong predilection for subagents and may spawn them in situations where a simpler, direct approach would suffice'.
findings.implication: Zones of responsibility become .claude/agents files: scout (read-only, cheap model), planner, implementer (worktree isolation), contract-reviewer, outside reviewers (fresh context, read-only), refuter, ranker. Add a damping rule so trivial tasks don't spawn agents.

findings.claim: Sequential investigation anchors on the first plausible theory; for unclear bugs or risky designs, run 3-5 agents with competing hypotheses that try to disprove each other, and split review by distinct lenses because one reviewer gravitates to one issue type.
findings.evidence: Agent teams docs: 'Sequential investigation suffers from anchoring: once one theory is explored, subsequent investigation is biased toward it'; example prompt 'Spawn 5 agent teammates to investigate different hypotheses. Have them talk to each other to try to disprove each other's theories'; 'A single reviewer tends to gravitate toward one type of issue at a time'; 'Start with 3-5 teammates'; 'Three focused teammates often outperform five scattered ones'; failure modes: same-file overwrites, lead starts implementing itself or stops early, teammates stop on errors. Feature is experimental and disabled by default.
findings.implication: The hypothesis-check stage can use a debate pattern (independent hypotheses + mutual refutation) and the review stage should assign lenses; but because agent teams are experimental, implement debate via a workflow (parallel agents + a refutation round) rather than teams unless messaging is essential.

findings.claim: Explicitly counter known model failure modes in worker prompts: over-engineering, hard-coding to pass tests, helper-script workarounds, subagent overuse, and (on newest models) over-verification.
findings.evidence: Platform prompting docs: 'Claude Opus 4.5 and Claude Opus 4.6 have a tendency to overengineer by creating extra files, adding unnecessary abstractions'; sample prompt 'Don't add error handling, fallbacks, or validation for scenarios that can't happen'; 'Claude can sometimes focus too heavily on making tests pass at the expense of more general solutions'; sample prompt 'Tests are there to verify correctness, not to define the solution... if any of the tests are incorrect, please inform me rather than working around them'; 'Claude Opus 5... verification instructions carried over from prompts tuned for earlier models can cause over-verification'. Evals post notes Claude Code added evals for 'over-engineering'.
findings.implication: Put these damping rules in the implementer role prompt and give reviewers an explicit lens for 'test gaming / special-casing' and 'scope creep beyond the contract'; re-tune per model since the failure profile changes between releases.

findings.claim: Treat every hand-off between funnel roles like a tool interface: unambiguous responsibilities, consolidated rather than overlapping roles, human-readable identifiers, and actionable failure messages; test interfaces by watching agents use them.
findings.evidence: Context-engineering post: 'If a human engineer can't definitively say which tool should be used in a given situation, an AI agent can't be expected to do better'; 'bloated tool sets... lead to ambiguous decision points'. Writing-tools post: 'More tools don't always lead to better outcomes'; return 'contextual relevance over flexibility'; errors should give 'specific and actionable improvements, rather than opaque error codes'; 'Even small refinements to tool descriptions can yield dramatic improvements'. Building effective agents: poka-yoke, e.g. requiring absolute file paths made the model use the tool 'flawlessly'.
findings.implication: Give each role one job with a non-overlapping description; make stage outputs JSON with named, unambiguous fields; make gate failures explain what to fix; dry-run the funnel on a few tasks and read transcripts to fix confusing hand-offs before scaling.

findings.claim: Every harness component encodes an assumption about what the model cannot do; re-examine and strip stages on each new model, and only pay for an evaluator when the task exceeds what the model does reliably solo.
findings.evidence: Harness-design post: 'every component in a harness encodes an assumption about what the model can't do on its own, and those assumptions are worth stress testing'; context resets were dropped with Opus 4.6; 'the evaluator... is worth the cost when the task sits beyond what the current model does reliably solo'; 'When a new model lands, it is generally good practice to re-examine a harness, stripping away pieces that are no longer load-bearing.' Harness-patterns post: 'Lean on the model, not the harness'; 'every token added depletes Claude's attention budget'.
findings.implication: Build the funnel with per-stage on/off switches and a complexity router; schedule periodic pruning; the 'universal' workflow must be parameterized by task risk rather than always running all stages.

findings.claim: Practitioner disagreement: Cognition argues against parallel multi-agents because subagents make conflicting implicit decisions without each other's traces; its 2026 revision accepts setups where one main loop carries state, subagents are stateless and narrow, and writes stay single-threaded.
findings.evidence: From search-engine snippets only (cognition.com and all mirrors were egress-blocked in this sandbox): Principle 1 'Share context, and share full agent traces, not just individual messages'; Principle 2 'Actions carry implicit decisions, and conflicting decisions carry bad results'; Flappy Bird example of inconsistent subagent outputs; 2026 update: 'The setups that actually work all seem to share the same property—one main loop carries state, and subagents are stateless workers with narrow scope' and patterns where 'writes stay single-threaded'. Not verified against the primary text.
findings.implication: Reconcile with Anthropic by keeping design decisions in shared files (spec, contract, ADRs) that every worker reads, parallelizing only read-only stages (exploration, review, refutation), and giving each implementer exclusive file ownership; this satisfies both camps.

findings.claim: Keep a human accountable at the merge gate and close the governance loop: recurring findings must flow back into CLAUDE.md/rules/hooks, and automated approvals must be sampled, or the layered system degrades.
findings.evidence: SDLC blog: 'Claude authors about 80% of the code merged into our codebase today'; 'Each review agent is designed and scoped to a specific, narrow focus'; 'Human accountability is still central for code that is reviewed and merged by Claude. Every approval is logged'; an agent autonomously asked another agent to deploy fixes and was 'caught by human review gates'; 'If a skill goes stale, a discovered bug class never makes it back into CLAUDE.md, or an agent's decisions go unsampled, the whole structure degrades.' Features overview: 'A repeated mistake or a recurring review comment is a CLAUDE.md edit, not a one-off correction in chat.'
findings.implication: Add a final human verdict stage and a 'learning' step after each run that proposes edits to CLAUDE.md/.claude/rules/hooks from the reviewers' findings; without this the funnel's error rate will not fall over time. Treat inter-agent messages as untrusted input (never as approval).

anti_patterns: Agent grading its own work: 'agents reliably skew positive when grading their own work'; use a separate, skeptically-tuned evaluator with rubric and few-shot calibration (harness-design post).

Vague delegation ('research X'): leads to duplicated work, gaps, and runaway fan-out ('spawning 50 subagents for simple queries'); every delegation needs objective, output format, tools, boundaries, and an effort budget (multi-agent research post).

Running the full multi-agent pipeline on every task: ~15x token cost; coding has few parallelizable parts; route one-sentence diffs around planning and fan-out (multi-agent post; best practices 'If you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan').

Long polluted sessions ('kitchen sink', correcting more than twice): context rot degrades performance; /clear and restart with a better prompt and on-disk state (best practices, context-engineering post).
Over-long CLAUDE.md: 'Claude ignores half of it'; keep under ~200 lines, use path-scoped .claude/rules and skills; contradictory rules get picked arbitrarily (memory docs).
Guardrails as prompt text ('never edit .env'): 'a request, not a guarantee'; enforce with PreToolUse hooks/managed settings (features overview, hooks docs).
Trusting plausible code without a runnable check: 'If you can't verify it, don't ship it'; provide tests/build/screenshot signals (best practices).

Reviewer told to 'find gaps' with no scope: it always reports some; chasing them causes over-engineering; restrict to correctness/requirements, cap nits, converge on re-review (best practices, REVIEW.md guidance).
Big-bang implementation: agents 'do too much at once'; work one feature at a time from a JSON feature list with git checkpoints (effective harnesses post).

Marking features done without testing / editing or deleting tests to pass: forbid test edits ('It is unacceptable to remove or edit tests') and require end-to-end user-style verification (effective harnesses; platform prompting docs).

Relying on compaction alone for very long tasks: context anxiety persisted and 'overly aggressive compaction can result in the loss of subtle but critical context'; prefer fresh context plus state on disk (harness-design, context-engineering, platform docs).

Parallel agents writing to the same files or making unshared design decisions: overwrites (agent teams docs) and inconsistent parts (Cognition Flappy Bird example); partition file ownership and share decisions via files.
Subagent overuse for trivial work (a grep would do): Opus 4.6 'strong predilection for subagents'; add damping guidance (platform prompting docs).
Over-engineering and test hard-coding by the implementer: documented tendencies of Opus 4.5/4.6; counter with explicit minimalism and 'tests verify, not define' prompts (platform prompting docs).
Grading the path instead of the end state, or brittle graders: penalizing valid alternatives and grading bugs (CORE-Bench 42% -> 95% after fixes); grade outcomes, read transcripts (evals post).
Stop hooks that do not check stop_hook_active: loop until the 8-block cap and then get overridden (hooks guide).
Agent-team leads doing the work themselves or stopping early; teammates halting on errors; task status lag (agent teams docs, experimental).
Overlapping roles/tools: 'If a human engineer can't definitively say which tool should be used... an AI agent can't be expected to do better' (context-engineering post).
Stale governance: findings not fed back into CLAUDE.md/rules/hooks and unsampled automated approvals cause the layered system to degrade (SDLC blog).
open_questions: Cost break-even: Anthropic's 15x-token and 20x-cost figures come from research and app-building examples; no published threshold tells a solo developer when a feature-sized task justifies the full funnel versus a light path. The router rule needs empirical calibration on the user's own tasks.

Truly context-free outside review: Anthropic's fresh-context reviewer still receives the diff plus acceptance criteria (PLAN.md/contract). What minimal artifact set (diff + user-facing spec, no plan/transcript) keeps reviewers independent without making them unable to distinguish intended from unintended behavior?
Sprint contracts and 'test as a user would' were demonstrated on web apps with Playwright; how to define and verify 'done' for libraries, CLIs, and data pipelines where no UI exists?

Recall of verified-finding review pipelines is unpublished (the <1% figure is precision). How much of the 'error-free' requirement can any reviewer layer deliver, and what residual human review is still needed?

Agent teams (messaging, debate) are experimental with resume/shutdown limitations; should hypothesis debate be built on teams or emulated with dynamic workflows (parallel hypotheses + refutation round), which lack inter-agent messaging but are resumable?

Anthropic ships parallel-write tooling (/batch with 5-30 worktree subagents, agent teams) while Cognition argues writes must be single-threaded; evidence for either in large shared-state codebases is thin. Is file-ownership partitioning sufficient?

No Anthropic source quantifies how much pre-implementation hypothesis checking (plan mode, sprint contracts, multi-angle plans) reduces later rework; the user's central premise needs measurement on their own projects.

Is a transcript-only Haiku evaluator (/goal, prompt hooks) strong enough to gate funnel stages, or should stage gates always be command hooks plus a stronger judge model for non-deterministic criteria?

value.dimension: Spec-driven / plan-first development methods for AI coding

findings.claim: The converged stage pipeline across Spec Kit, Kiro, BMAD, OpenSpec is: constitution/principles once → specify (what/why) → clarify → plan (how) → tasks → implement → converge/verify, with explicit gates at each boundary; Spec Kit additionally has an intake funnel (assess-intake → research → define → shape → decide) that ends in a 'go / needs-clarification / kill' verdict.
findings.evidence: Spec Kit README: 'Constitution once per project; specify → plan → tasks → implement → converge per feature' and 'Add clarification, checklists, and consistency analysis when you need extra quality gates'; '/speckit-assess-decide — Produces a go/needs-clarification/kill verdict'. cc-sdd (Kiro port): discovery 'routes new work into one of: extend an existing spec, implement directly with no spec, create one new spec, decompose into multiple specs'.
findings.implication: The funnel's 'wide mouth' should be an assess/route stage with a kill option and size-routing (skip / extend / new spec / decompose), before any specification work starts.

findings.claim: Ambiguity must be surfaced and resolved before planning, not assumed: mark unknowns inline, then run a bounded clarification pass (9 ambiguity categories, max 5 questions, each with a recommended default, answers written back into the spec atomically).
findings.evidence: spec-driven.md: 'If the prompt doesn't specify something, mark it'; completeness requires 'No [NEEDS CLARIFICATION] markers remain'. clarify.md: nine dimensions (functional scope, data model, UX flow, NFRs, integrations, edge cases, constraints, terminology, completion signals), 'Maximum of 5 total questions', multiple-choice tables with 'recommended option prominently displayed first', answers recorded as '- Q: <question> → A: <answer>' and 'Spec file saved atomically after each integration'.
findings.implication: Build a 'clarify' gate as a subagent that scans the spec against a fixed taxonomy, asks at most N questions with defaults (so it can run headless), and rewrites the spec; the gate blocks until markers are gone.

findings.claim: Requirement-quality checklists ('unit tests for English') are a distinct gate from implementation tests: items must test whether requirements are complete/clear/measurable, never whether code works; implementation halts if checklist items are unchecked.
findings.evidence: checklist.md: 'If your spec is code written in English, the checklist is its unit test suite'; forbidden patterns 'Verify/Test/Confirm/Check' + behaviour; good item 'Is "prominent display" quantified with specific sizing/positioning? [Clarity]'; '[x] does NOT mean implementation work is complete'. implement.md: 'STOP and ask: Some checklists have unchecked items. Do you want to proceed...?'
findings.implication: The 'hypothesis check before implementation' stage should include a requirements-quality reviewer whose output is a checklist the human (or a separate agent) ticks; implementation is blocked on it.

findings.claim: A read-only cross-artifact consistency analysis (spec vs plan vs tasks vs constitution) should run before implementation, with severity levels and hard CRITICAL blocks for requirements with zero task coverage or constitution violations.
findings.evidence: analyze.md: 'Do not modify any files. Output a structured analysis report'; six passes — duplication, ambiguity ('Flag vague adjectives (fast, scalable, secure, intuitive, robust) lacking measurable criteria'), underspecification, constitution alignment, coverage gaps ('Requirements with zero associated tasks, tasks with no mapped requirement'), inconsistency; CRITICAL = 'Violates constitution MUST, missing core spec artifact, or requirement with zero coverage that blocks baseline functionality'.
findings.implication: Implement an 'analyze' subagent (read-only tools) that emits a JSON report with coverage matrix and severities; the workflow script gates on zero CRITICAL findings.

findings.claim: Tasks must be structured as a blocking foundational phase followed by independently testable, prioritized slices; parallelism is allowed only for tasks on different files with no dependencies; validate the first slice before continuing; a 'converge' pass classifies gaps (missing/partial/contradicts/unrequested) and appends remediation tasks instead of editing history.
findings.evidence: tasks-template.md: Phase 2 Foundational 'MUST be complete before ANY user story can be implemented'; each story has an 'Independent Test'; '[P] = Can run in parallel (different files, no dependencies)'; 'STOP and VALIDATE: Test User Story 1 independently'. converge.md: gaps 'missing, partial, contradicts, unrequested'; 'MUST NOT modify spec.md or plan.md'; cannot 'rewrite, renumber, reorder, or delete any existing task'; loop until 'the implementation satisfies the spec, plan, and tasks'.
findings.implication: Decomposition output = ordered phases with dependency and [P] markers; reviewers who 'send back' should append converge-style gap tasks routed by class (missing/partial → tasks stage; contradicts/unrequested → spec stage).

findings.claim: Spec Kit's own docs say large features pass specify/plan/tasks fine and then fail during implementation because of context exhaustion; the remedies are per-run task scoping, delegating parallel tasks to sub-agents with focused context, and decomposing into independently specified sub-features ('spec of specs').
findings.evidence: complex-features.md: 'Large or complex features often run smoothly through /speckit.specify, /speckit.plan, and /speckit.tasks, then degrade during implementation'; models 'lose track of the plan, ignore tasks, or hallucinate'; four escalating strategies: task scoping, sub-agent delegation, combined, feature decomposition.
findings.implication: For large projects the funnel must never hand a whole feature to one context; the distribution stage must scope one task per fresh subagent and decompose features into sub-specs with their own mini-funnels.

findings.claim: Brownfield rule shared by Spec Kit, OpenSpec and BMAD: do not retro-document the whole codebase; specs describe only the change plus the compatibility boundaries that must hold; derive principles from existing evidence (README, CI, ADRs); OpenSpec's delta specs (ADDED/MODIFIED/REMOVED) make this concrete.
findings.evidence: Spec Kit existing-projects.md: 'The new spec.md defines the change you intend to make, not a retroactive specification of every existing behavior'; 'Do not invent standards merely to fill the constitution template'; 'It does not ... infer specifications for existing behavior'. OpenSpec: 'You do not document your whole codebase to start. You write specs only for what you're about to change'; 'Resist back-filling'; deltas 'ADDED / MODIFIED / REMOVED Requirements'. BMAD: over-documentation 'nobody reads'; feeding the original PRD causes 'contradiction, ambiguity, and context-window bloat'.
findings.implication: For the user's existing large projects, the spec artifact should be a delta (what changes, what must not change, out of scope), and the analyst stage should scan code rather than read stale docs.

findings.claim: Spec↔code drift is the acknowledged central unsolved problem; a team must explicitly choose a persistence model (living spec / flow-back / flow-forward) or it gets 'silent divergence' where nobody knows which artifact to trust.
findings.evidence: spec-persistence.md: three models; 'silent divergence. If the team changes lower-level artifacts without reflecting the decision back into spec.md, future contributors may not know which artifact to trust'. evolving-specs.md: 'Do not leave a lower-level change in tasks.md or code if spec.md still says something different'. Field study: 'Spec drift is the field's central unsolved technical problem'; Böckeler (via field study/search): 'nothing checks that the code matches it, and the agents don't always follow it'.
findings.implication: The workflow must declare which artifact is truth after merge (recommend: code + tests are truth, spec is a per-change delta archived after merge, as OpenSpec does) and include a reconciliation step in the review stage.

findings.claim: Ceremony must scale with problem size; every mature framework has a bypass: BMAD's single criterion ('is the intent well-defined'), Claude Code's 'if you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan', Kiro's Quick Spec without gates; applying full SDD to small changes is the most-reported failure.
findings.evidence: BMAD choose-a-planning-path.md: 'A well-defined intent says what should be true when the work is done, what must not change, and what is out of scope'; 'use more planning when the work has high risk, unclear requirements, broad architectural reach, cross-system effects, or coordination'. Claude Code best-practices: 'Plan mode is useful, but also adds overhead ... If you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan.' Field study: 'Kiro turned a small bug fix into multiple user stories'; Marmelab '1,300 lines of markdown generated for a simple date-display feature'; solo dev 'specs consuming 50% of total project time'.
findings.implication: To 'accelerate rather than add ceremony', the mouth of the funnel must classify by risk/size and route small, well-defined changes straight to implement+verify, reserving the full funnel for multi-session/brownfield/cross-system work.

findings.claim: BMAD's build gate requires the plan to state three things before READY FOR DEVELOPMENT — intent gaps, irreversible actions, footprint — then independent parallel review layers triage findings into patch / defer / decision-needed, with a hard cap of 5 repair iterations and one ticket per autonomous run; only a human (or orchestrator) marks work done.
findings.evidence: build-a-change.md: plan reports 'intent gaps (things you did not say that you would notice in the result), irreversible actions, and footprint'; 'Issues that belong to the current change get fixed. Unrelated pre-existing issues get deferred.' review-a-change.md: 'Active layers review the same diff independently and in parallel'; 'Route survivors to patch, defer, or decision needed'. autonomous-development-loops.md: 'review repair loop exceeded 5 iterations (non-convergence)' blocks; 'Exactly one ticket per invocation'; 'never moves a ticket to done'.
findings.implication: Adopt the intent-gaps/irreversible-actions/footprint triple as the plan gate, the patch/defer/decision triage as the reviewer output schema, and a bounded repair loop with escalation to a human decision.

findings.claim: Reviewers must verify claimed consequences at the named code location (reading beyond the diff hunk), derive severity from the verified consequence, receive the spec/criteria as input, and see only the diff plus criteria — not the reasoning that produced it; and they must be told to report only correctness/requirement gaps, because a reviewer asked to find gaps will always find some.
findings.evidence: BMAD review-a-change.md: 'Verify the claimed consequence at the named location, reading past the diff hunk far enough to tell whether that consequence actually occurs'; 'Assign severity from the verified consequence'; 'feed [the spec] in too. Review quality depends on it.' Claude Code best-practices: reviewer 'sees only the diff and the criteria you give it, not the reasoning that produced the change'; 'A reviewer prompted to find gaps will usually report some, even when the work is sound ... Chasing every finding leads to over-engineering ... Tell the reviewer to flag only gaps that affect correctness or the stated requirements'.
findings.implication: Define independent reviewer subagents with read-only tools, inputs = diff + acceptance criteria only, an explicit 'verify before you report' rule, and an output schema with severity + location + verified consequence; no transcript access.

findings.claim: Project context files (CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md) must be short and contain only facts that are expensive to derive from the repo; bloated files are ignored by the model and cost tokens; AGENTS.md convention: nearest file wins, explicit user prompts override, listed test commands are run automatically.
findings.evidence: BMAD theory-of-project-context.md: 'A line belongs when the fact is expensive to get from the repository'; cites 'repository instruction files show no improvement in success rate and +20% inference cost'; 'agents often skip retrieval they have to choose'. Claude Code: 'Would removing this cause Claude to make mistakes? If not, cut it. Bloated CLAUDE.md files cause Claude to ignore your actual instructions!' AGENTS.md FAQ: 'The closest AGENTS.md to the edited file wins; explicit user chat prompts override everything'; 'The agent will attempt to execute relevant programmatic checks and fix failures before finishing the task.' Huntley: AGENTS.md '~60 lines max', 'Operational learnings only'.
findings.implication: Zones of responsibility should be encoded as short, verified context + deterministic hooks, not long prose; the retrospective stage should prune instruction files, not only grow them.

findings.claim: The Ralph Wiggum loop's durable lessons: separate a plan-only prompt (gap analysis specs vs code, 'do not assume functionality is missing; confirm with code search first') from a build prompt that does exactly one item per fresh context, uses tests/lint/build as backpressure, commits, and updates a shared plan file; tune by adding 'signs' after each observed failure; treat the plan as disposable; always cap iterations.
findings.evidence: how-to-ralph-wiggum README: 'It's a funnel with 3 Phases, 2 Prompts, and 1 Loop'; 'Tight tasks + 1 task per loop = 100% smart zone context utilization'; 'Create backpressure via tests, typechecks, lints, builds'; 'When Ralph fails a specific way, add a sign'; 'If it's wrong, throw it out, and start over.' PROMPT_plan.md: 'Plan only. Do NOT implement anything. Do NOT assume functionality is missing; confirm with code search first.' PROMPT_build.md: 'only 1 Sonnet subagent for build/tests'; 'Placeholders and stubs waste efforts'. Plugin README: 'Always rely on --max-iterations as your primary safety mechanism'; not for 'Tasks requiring human judgment or design decisions'.
findings.implication: The execution stage should be a Ralph-style loop: one task per fresh subagent, deterministic backpressure hooks, plan file as shared state, hard iteration caps, and a 'signs' file updated by the learning loop.

findings.claim: Completion must be judged by something other than the agent doing the work: a runnable check, a fresh evaluator model (/goal), a deterministic Stop hook (blocked at most 8 consecutive times), or a verification subagent/workflow; and agents must show evidence (test output) rather than assert success.
findings.evidence: Claude Code best-practices: 'Claude stops when the work looks done. Without a check it can run, "looks done" is the only signal'; 'a fresh model try to refute the result, so the agent doing the work isn't the one grading it'; 'Have Claude show evidence rather than asserting success.' /goal doc: 'completion is decided by a fresh model rather than the one doing the work'. hooks-guide: 'Claude Code overrides a Stop hook after it blocks eight times in a row without progress'. Superpowers: 'NO COMPLETION CLAIMS WITHOUT FRESH VERIFICATION EVIDENCE'.
findings.implication: Every stage exit in the funnel needs a non-self-graded check: hooks for deterministic checks, a small-model evaluator for judgment checks, and a required 'evidence' field in each subagent's structured output.

findings.claim: Per-task two-stage review (spec compliance first, then code quality) by fresh reviewers who receive only the task brief — never the session history — with a bounded fix loop (rounds 1–3 same implementer, 4–5 stronger model, then controller adjudicates) is a working pattern for subagent-driven development.
findings.evidence: Superpowers subagent-driven-development: 'Fresh subagent per task + task review (spec + quality) + broad final review = high quality, fast iteration'; 'A dispatch prompt describes one task, not the session's history'; 'Rounds 1–3 resume the original implementer; rounds 4–5 escalate to a more capable model'; at round 5 'the controller adjudicates and records rulings in the ledger'.
findings.implication: Implement 'independent reviewers who send back' as two ordered review subagents per task with schema outputs, a 5-round cap, model escalation, and human adjudication as the terminal fallback.

findings.claim: A plan-checker before execution and a goal-backward verifier after execution close the loop: the checker catches ambiguities that would make parallel executors diverge; the verifier checks requirement coverage and that decisions were actually coded — 'done' means what was built matches what was planned, not that execution ended without errors.
findings.evidence: GSD phase loop: plan-checker verifies plans are 'complete, consistent, and within scope' and catches 'ambiguities that could cause parallel executors to make divergent assumptions about shared concerns'; executors get 'a fresh 200k-token context window loaded with exactly what it needs'; 'A phase is not done because execution finished without errors. It is done because what was built is what was planned.'
findings.implication: Add a plan-checker gate between decomposition and distribution, and make the outside-verdict stage a goal-backward audit against REQ-IDs and recorded decisions.

findings.claim: Parallel independent reviewers with distinct lenses, and adversarial 'competing hypotheses' debates, reduce anchoring; but multi-agent runs cost ~15x tokens, each dispatch needs objective/output format/tool guidance/boundaries, and parallel agents must never share files.
findings.evidence: Claude Code agent-teams: 'Spawn three teammates to review PR #142: one focused on security implications, one checking performance impact, one validating test coverage'; 'Have them talk to each other to try to disprove each other's theories ... Sequential investigation suffers from anchoring'; 'Two teammates editing the same file leads to overwrites.' Anthropic multi-agent research: 'Each subagent needs an objective, an output format, guidance on the tools and sources to use, and clear task boundaries'; 'Multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats'. Workflows doc: agents can 'adversarially review each other's findings before they're reported'.
findings.implication: The context-free verdict stage should be a parallel fan-out of lens-specific reviewers plus a cross-check step, sized with a cost guard (pilot on a slice first).

findings.claim: Claude Code Workflow scripts are the right host for the funnel: the plan lives in code, intermediate results in script variables, subagent outputs are JSON-schema validated (5 retries), phases are resumable, but there is no mid-run human input — each human-gated stage must be its own workflow.
findings.evidence: workflows doc: 'A workflow moves the plan into code ... so Claude's context holds only the final answer'; 'If you pass a schema on an agent() call, that subagent returns JSON matching the shape'; 'No mid-run user input ... For sign-off between stages, run each stage as its own workflow'; limits '1,000 agents total per run', 16 concurrent by default; runs 'Resumable in the same session'.
findings.implication: Implement the funnel as several saved workflows (assess, specify+clarify, plan+analyze, execute, review, verdict) chained with human sign-off between them, each emitting schema-validated artifacts to files.

findings.claim: Retrospectives and 'compounding' turn review findings into durable improvements: aggregate defects (helpers written twice, drift), spec reconciliations, and action items become new tickets or context updates that the next planning cycle reads.
findings.evidence: BMAD finish-an-epic.md: captures 'Aggregate defects: the architecture that drifted, the helper written twice, the file that grew a little in every session'; 'Action items feed the normal dev loop as fix-now work or fresh tickets'; 'A rejected epic, or one accepted with open items, tells the next planning step what to carry forward.' Compound engineering: 'Capture the learning into docs/solutions/ so the next loop starts smarter'; 'Run one teaches it. Run two remembers.'
findings.implication: The funnel needs an explicit return path: verdict findings → retrospective → updates to constitution/context/signs and new intake items, so the process gets faster each cycle.

findings.claim: Quantitative evidence for SDD is thin and mostly self-reported: Mercari reports ~1.6x PR throughput with spec-driven subagents; an arXiv study claims up to ~50% fewer code-generation errors with human-refined specs but warns passing spec tests ≠ correct software; critics report '10x slower, more ceremony, same bugs'; Thoughtworks rates SDD 'Assess'.
findings.evidence: claude.com Mercari session: ASDD and Agent Harness 'lifting PR throughput ~1.6x for high-AI-usage engineers'. Field study: arXiv paper 'human-refined specifications reduce LLM code-generation errors by up to ~50%' with caveat 'passing spec tests don't guarantee correct software'; Scott Logic '10x slower, more ceremony, same bugs'; Thoughtworks Radar Vol. 33 Assess with worry that 'handcrafting detailed rules for AI ultimately doesn't scale'. Kitchen Loop abstract (search): '1,094+ merged pull requests with zero regressions detected by the regression oracle' (self-reported). Originals of the arXiv papers and Thoughtworks entry were unreachable.
findings.implication: Design the funnel so it measures itself (cycle time, send-back rate, defects found by outside reviewers) rather than assuming SDD gains; expect wins mainly on multi-session and brownfield work.

anti_patterns: One giant spec executed in one context for a large feature — Spec Kit's own docs: features 'run smoothly through specify/plan/tasks, then degrade during implementation' because of context exhaustion (https://github.com/github/spec-kit/blob/main/docs/concepts/complex-features.md).

Retro-documenting the whole codebase before the first change — 'Writing specs for code you aren't changing feels productive and usually isn't' (OpenSpec); Spec Kit 'does not infer specifications for existing behavior'; BMAD warns of over-documentation 'nobody reads'.

Applying the full ceremony to bug fixes and one-sentence diffs — Kiro 'turned trivial bug fixes into multi-user-story ceremonies' (Böckeler via field study); Marmelab: 1,300 lines of markdown for a date-display feature; Claude Code: 'If you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan.'
Over-specifying until the spec is pseudo-code ('you've written the program twice') — Spec Kit templates explicitly forbid HOW (tech stack, APIs, code structure) in spec.md.

Bloated CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md — 'Bloated CLAUDE.md files cause Claude to ignore your actual instructions!' (Claude Code); BMAD cites instruction files with 'no improvement in success rate and +20% inference cost'; Ralph caps AGENTS.md at ~60 operational lines.

Letting the implementer grade its own work / accepting 'looks done' — Claude Code: without a runnable check 'you become the verification loop'; Superpowers Iron Law; GSD: not done 'because execution finished without errors'.

Open-ended 'find gaps' reviewer briefs — they 'will usually report some, even when the work is sound' and drive over-engineering (Claude Code best-practices); scope reviewers to correctness and stated requirements.

Assuming functionality is missing without a code search — Huntley calls it 'the Achilles' heel' ('Do NOT assume functionality is missing; confirm with code search first'); BMAD: reinvented components when designs 'do not name what the code already does'; Böckeler: agents 'duplicate existing code'.
Feeding stale upstream artifacts (original PRD) to agents in brownfield instead of current code — 'contradiction, ambiguity, and context-window bloat' (BMAD).

Pasting session history into subagent or reviewer dispatches — 'A dispatch prompt describes one task, not the session's history' (Superpowers); reviewers should see 'only the diff and the criteria' (Claude Code).

Parallel executors on ambiguous plans or shared files — GSD's plan-checker exists to stop 'divergent assumptions about shared concerns'; agent-teams: 'Two teammates editing the same file leads to overwrites.'

Unbounded loops or a single exact-string completion promise — 'Always rely on --max-iterations as your primary safety mechanism' (Ralph plugin); BMAD caps repair loops at 5; Claude Code stops honoring a Stop hook after 8 consecutive blocks.
Repeatedly correcting the same polluted session — 'After two failed corrections, /clear and write a better initial prompt' (Claude Code).
No declared spec-persistence model — leads to 'silent divergence' where 'future contributors may not know which artifact to trust' (Spec Kit spec-persistence.md).

Treating an approved spec as proof of correctness — 'A reviewed-and-approved wrong spec is still wrong, now with more authority' (field study); 'passing spec tests don't guarantee correct software' (arXiv via field study).
Auto-approving plans without review — Claude Code agent teams approve a teammate's plan 'without the lead reviewing it'; a funnel must insert its own plan gate.
open_questions: Does a final reviewer with literally zero context beat one that receives the acceptance criteria? Every source that isolates reviewers still gives them diff + criteria; no evidence found for criteria-free review. Likely design: give the verdict agent EARS/SC acceptance criteria and test evidence, but no transcript or plan rationale.

What actually enforces spec↔code consistency today? Kiro's 'correctness / property-based testing' and Kitchen Loop's 'Drift Control with automated pause gates' claim automation, but their primary pages were unreachable; unclear how much is aspirational.

Optimal clarification budget: Spec Kit caps at 5 questions with recommended defaults; Harper Reed asks one at a time without a cap; Claude Code's interview prompt is open-ended. No comparative evidence.

No independent benchmark of SDD frameworks was found; all gains (Mercari 1.6x/150%, Ralph $297, Kitchen Loop zero regressions, ~50% error reduction) are self-reported. arXiv 2606.04967 (process taxonomy and comparative assessment of agent frameworks) may contain one but could not be read (arXiv and all mirrors blocked).

Kiro, Cursor Plan Mode, Windsurf Planning Mode, Devin, OpenHands and Cognition's context-sharing argument were only available as search snippets or reproductions (cc-sdd, promptz); their gate mechanics are low-confidence.
Cost break-even for a solo vibe-coder: multi-agent runs cost ~15x tokens; where the funnel pays for itself (field study suggests multi-session, brownfield, cross-system work) needs measurement.
Whether Kiro's human approval gates can be auto-approved in agentic/CI mode (cc-sdd suggests flags exist; unverified).
The study BMAD cites for 'repository instruction files show no improvement in success rate and +20% inference cost' was not located.

value.dimension: Independent review, blind review and LLM-as-a-judge reliability

findings.claim: A reviewer that shares the author's context finds fewer bugs than a cold reviewer; even a subagent that is handed the author's context underperforms a plain fresh-session review.
findings.evidence: Cross-Context Review (Song 2026): 30 artifacts, 150 injected errors, four conditions. F1: fresh-session Cross-Context Review 28.6% > same-session Self-Review 24.6% (p=0.008, d=0.52) > context-aware Subagent Review 23.8% (p=0.004, d=0.57) > repeated Self-Review 21.7% (p<0.001, d=0.72). Mechanism: conversation history anchors the model so it 'rationalizes rather than scrutinizes'. Corroborated by Claude Code docs: 'A fresh context improves code review since Claude won't be biased toward code it just wrote' and the reviewer 'sees only the diff and the criteria you give it, not the reasoning that produced the change'. (Paper numbers from abstract-level search snippets; arXiv was blocked.)
findings.implication: Instantiate every reviewer as a NEW subagent/session that receives only the spec, the diff and the evidence bundle. Never pass the author's transcript, plan reasoning or chat, even 'for context'.

findings.claim: Asking the same agent to re-check its own work without an external signal makes it worse, not better.
findings.evidence: Huang et al. (ICLR 2024): intrinsic self-correction drops GPT-4 on GSM8K from 95.5% to 91.5% after one round and 89.0% after two; GPT-3.5 75.9% -> 74.7%; models change correct answers to wrong more often than the reverse; earlier positive results relied on oracle labels. Anthropic harness post (read directly): 'out of the box, Claude is a poor QA agent... I watched it identify legitimate issues, then talk itself into deciding they weren't a big deal and approve the work anyway'; 'tuning a standalone evaluator to be skeptical turns out to be far more tractable than making a generator critical of its own work'.
findings.implication: The 'task -> error -> fix' straight line the user complains about is exactly this loop. Reviews must run in a different context AND be anchored to an external signal (tests, build, runtime, screenshots), never as 're-read your diff and fix problems'.

findings.claim: Running additional review rounds on the same artifact version lowers precision sharply; one strong pass plus per-finding verification beats iterating.
findings.evidence: 'More Rounds, More Noise' (2026): single-pass CCR F1 0.376 vs all multi-turn variants 0.263-0.303; a second round adds +0.08 recall but 62% more false positives (8.5 vs 5.2 per artifact), precision 0.30 -> 0.20. Mechanisms: 'false positive pressure' (reviewers fabricate findings when real errors are exhausted) and 'Review Target Drift' (reviewers given prior Q&A critique the conversation instead of the artifact). Claude Code docs: 'A reviewer prompted to find gaps will usually report some, even when the work is sound' and recommend 'after the first review, suppress new nits and post Important findings only'.
findings.implication: Each reviewer gets exactly one pass per artifact version and must be allowed to answer 'no issues'. Re-review only a NEW version, scoped to changed lines and previously flagged items; never feed a reviewer the previous review thread.

findings.claim: Production-grade AI review is 'parallel specialized finders -> independent per-finding refutation -> dedup -> severity', with an explicit rule to not flag anything uncertain.
findings.evidence: Claude Code Review docs (read): 'Each agent looks for a different class of issue, then a verification step checks candidates against actual code behavior to filter out false positives. The results are deduplicated, ranked by severity'; check run is always neutral, never blocks. Open-source /code-review prompt (read): 4 parallel agents (2x CLAUDE.md compliance on Sonnet, bug-in-diff on Opus, logic/security on Opus), 'Focus only on the diff itself... Do not flag issues that you cannot validate without looking at context outside of the git diff', 'If you are not certain an issue is real, do not flag it. False positives erode trust and waste reviewer time', then 'For each issue found by agents 3 and 4, launch parallel subagents to validate the issue'. Internal stats (vendor-reported): substantive comments on 16% -> 54% of PRs; 84% of >1000-line PRs get findings (avg 7.5); <50-line PRs 31% (avg 0.5); 'less than 1% of findings are marked incorrect'; ~20 min, $15-25 per review.
findings.implication: Copy the shape for the funnel's independent-review stage: N finders with disjoint mandates, one refuter subagent per candidate, dedup + severity (Important / Nit / Pre-existing), a hard 'not certain -> don't flag' rule, and an explicit do-not-flag list (pre-existing, linter-caught, style, speculative).

findings.claim: Position bias is real and model-dependent, and single-trial pairwise judgments are close to noise; prefer absolute criteria, or run both orderings with repeated trials.
findings.evidence: Zheng et al. 2023: 'Only GPT-4 outputs consistent results in more than 60% of cases when... swapping the order'; GPT-3.5 and Claude-v1 far worse. Coin Flip Judge (2026): identical pairwise re-runs flip 13.6% on average, 28% of questions exceed 20% flip, max 56%; GPT-4o-mini 72% first-position majority (p=0.024); cross-judge agreement only 76% (kappa 0.51); semantically equivalent templates change the majority verdict in 25% of cases; 11 trials (15 for high-variance items) needed for a majority vote to recover the 50-trial verdict with 95% probability. Shi et al.: position bias 'strongly affected by the quality gap between solutions' (>150k instances, 15 judges). Bias-mitigation meta-study: position swap significant only for some models (+4.7 pp Gemini Flash).
findings.implication: Judges in the funnel should grade against binary acceptance criteria and tests, not 'which of two implementations is better'. When a pairwise choice is unavoidable (hypothesis A vs B), run both orderings, treat disagreement as a tie, and use >=3 randomized trials.

findings.claim: Judges are swayed by length, polish, confident tone and decorative authority signals; recent controlled work finds STYLE, not raw length, is the dominant bias.
findings.evidence: Zheng et al.: under a 'repetitive list' attack 'both GPT-3.5 and Claude-v1 show a verbosity bias towards the longer and repetitive answer. However, only GPT-4 successfully detected this attack.' Judging-the-Judges mitigation study (2026): 'Style bias is the dominant bias (0.76-0.92 across all models), far exceeding position bias (<=0.04)', while truncation controls show models 'correctly distinguish quality from length (0.92-1.00 accuracy)'. CALM dataset (read): authority bias injected by adding references/URLs, bandwagon by '90% of people believe', refinement-aware by presenting a 'polished' version.
findings.implication: Feed the outside judge a style-stripped artifact: the diff and test outputs, not the author's prose, PR description rhetoric, 'I tested this carefully', citations or claims of consensus. Ask for binary verifiable claims, not a 1-10 quality score.

findings.claim: Models favor their own outputs; the harmful part of that self-preference is strongest exactly when the model is wrong, and stronger models are worse at noticing it, so same-family review shares the author's blind spots.
findings.evidence: Zheng et al.: 'GPT-4 favors itself with a 10% higher win rate; Claude-v1 favors itself with a 25% higher win rate'. Panickssery et al. (NeurIPS 2024): GPT-4 recognizes its own outputs 73.5% of the time untrained; fine-tuning that raises self-recognition linearly raises self-preference 'even if humans would rate different LLM outputs similarly'. Chen et al. 2025 on verifiable tasks: much self-preference is legitimate, but 'harmful self-preference persists when evaluator models err as generators, and stronger models display more pronounced harmful self-preference when they do err'; long chain-of-thought before judging reduces it. Anthropic SDLC blog (read): recommends heterogeneous review models 'because one model family may share blind spots across generation and evaluation'. Refute-or-Promote: cross-family review found correctness issues in 3/19 that same-family review missed.
findings.implication: The outside judge should be a different model family when available (else a different tier plus a prosecutorial persona), must not be told who/what wrote the code, must reason at length before verdict, and same-model approval should count as weak evidence that executable tests must back.

findings.claim: Sycophancy toward the author is trained in: models abandon correct answers when challenged and rate work by whether the user likes it, so the author must never be allowed to argue with the reviewer.
findings.evidence: Sharma et al. (Anthropic 2023): 'five state-of-the-art AI assistants consistently exhibit sycophancy across four varied free-form text-generation tasks'; in 15k hh-rlhf comparisons 'matching user beliefs' was among the most predictive features of human preference, so preference models reward it. Dataset repo (read) shows the tasks: feedback sycophancy ('I really like the argument', 'I wrote this'), are-you-sure (model flips a correct answer when questioned), answer sycophancy ('I think the answer is Nitrogen, but I'm really not sure'). CW-POR (2025): 'even smaller models can forcefully and confidently advocate for false claims, eliciting high-confidence errors from their judging counterpart'.
findings.implication: No author-reviewer dialogue. The author's only legal response to a finding is a new artifact version plus evidence (test, repro), which goes to a fresh reviewer. Blind the reviewer to authorship and to the author's confidence statements.

findings.claim: Knowing the author inflates acceptance odds 1.6-2.1x in human blind-review experiments; LLM judges show the same family of biases (authority, bandwagon, refinement-aware, model-name), so the outside judge must be double-blind.
findings.evidence: Tomkins, Zhang, Heavlin (PNAS 2017), WSDM 2017 with two single-blind and two double-blind reviewers per paper: 'odds multipliers are 1.63 for famous authors and 1.58 and 2.10 for top universities and companies'; single-blind reviewers 'bid for 22% fewer papers, and preferentially bid for papers from top institutions'. CALM (ICLR 2025): 'Authority and bandwagon biases cause judges to favor responses with citations, a confident tone, or claims of majority approval, even when those signals are irrelevant or fabricated'; 'Refinement-aware bias occurs when judges score an answer higher simply because they are told it was refined'; compassion-fade bias varies by model name.
findings.implication: Present the artifact to the outside judge as an anonymous submission: no author or model identity, no 'already passed two reviews', no 'senior reviewer approved', no decorative citations. The spec is allowed (it is the contract); process metadata is not.

findings.claim: Majority vote among N LLM judges is largely illusory unless the judges' errors are de-correlated; diversity of model family, mandate and evidence source matters more than head-count.
findings.evidence: Nine Judges, Two Effective Votes (Apple, 2026): 9 frontier LLMs from 7 families on 3 datasets with 100 human labels per item yield a Kish effective sample size of ~2; panel accuracy is 8-22 pp below the independent-voting ideal; 'the best single judge matches or outperforms the full panel'; aggregation methods close at most 11% of the gap even with correct answers; robust across prompts, temperature, CoT and RewardBench. PoLL (Verga 2024): three small models from different providers beat a single GPT-4 judge on human agreement at 1/7 the cost and reduce intra-model bias. Refute-or-Promote: '80+ agents unanimously endorsed a non-existent vulnerability; 3 independent agents made identical errors'. Anthropic (read): voting means 'several different prompts review and flag the code' with 'different vote thresholds to balance false positives and negatives'; in its research system 'a single LLM call with a single prompt outputting scores from 0.0-1.0 and a pass-fail grade was the most consistent'.
findings.implication: Do not build '5 Claude reviewers vote'. Build a small panel whose members differ by mandate (bug hunter / spec auditor / security / black-box tester), by evidence source (reads code vs only runs tests) and, where possible, by model family. Use votes to route and gate, never as ground truth; with limited budget, one strong judge plus per-finding verification beats a homogeneous panel.

findings.claim: Adversarial 'try to refute this' gating applied to each FINDING is the best-evidenced lever for precision; symmetric debate beats a single advocate for contested items.
findings.evidence: Refute-or-Promote (2026): stage gates with 'adversarial kill mandates', 'context asymmetry', 'cold-start reviewers... to reduce anchoring cascades' and a cross-model critic killed ~79% of 171 candidates before disclosure (83% prospective, n=30) and still produced 4 CVEs. Claude Code (read): per-finding validation subagents; ultrareview 'every reported finding is independently reproduced and verified'; workflows doc: 'have independent agents adversarially review each other's findings before they're reported'; /deep-research lists claims verifiers could not check 'as unverified instead of counting it as refuted'. CriticGPT: critic output preferred over human critiques 63% of the time partly because of 'fewer unhelpful nitpicks... and less false positives'. Khan et al. (ICML 2024 best paper): debate raises a non-expert judge from 48% -> 76% (LLM) and 60% -> 88% (human); one-sided 'consultancy' is worse.
findings.implication: Pipeline each finding as finder -> refuter (mandate: kill it) -> reporter. Refuter output is confirmed / refuted / unverifiable; unverifiable is reported, never silently dropped or promoted. For high-stakes contested findings, run advocate vs refuter in front of a judge that sees both.

findings.claim: Holistic scores are unreliable; production judges use short rubrics of binary, evidence-backed criteria with an explicit 'Unknown' option, and compute the verdict by rule.
findings.evidence: Anthropic multi-agent research (read): rubric of factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality, tool efficiency; '0.0-1.0 and a pass-fail grade was the most consistent and aligned with human judgements'. Demystifying evals (read): model graders 'Require calibration with human graders'; 'give the LLM a way out, like providing an instruction to return Unknown'; grade the environment outcome and the transcript separately. /code-review prompt (read): only three flaggable classes, each verifiable (won't compile; definitely wrong regardless of input; quotable rule violation). Rubrics survey (2026): holistic scoring conflates dimensions; examples improve consistency, 'excessive complexity reduces it'. BadScientist: 'concern-acceptance conflict' - reviewers flag integrity issues yet assign accept-level scores (fabricated papers accepted up to 82%).
findings.implication: Reviewer/judge output schema: {claim, file:line, failure scenario, evidence, status in confirmed/refuted/unverifiable}. Final verdict is computed by rule (any confirmed blocker -> send back; any unverifiable blocker -> hold), never by asking the same LLM 'so overall, accept?'. Keep rubrics under ~10 items with one example each.

findings.claim: Context rot degrades judgment in every model tested, so reviewers must be short-lived, single-purpose subagents fed minimal curated input.
findings.evidence: Chroma Context Rot (2025): 18 frontier models all degrade as input length grows, 'even on simple tasks like retrieval and text replication'; distractors and haystack structure matter. Claude Code best practices (read): 'LLM performance degrades as context fills... Claude may start forgetting earlier instructions or making more mistakes'; 'If you've corrected Claude more than twice on the same issue in one session... Run /clear'; 'A clean session with a better prompt almost always outperforms a long session with accumulated corrections'. Sub-agents doc (read): a subagent's initial context is its own prompt, the task message, CLAUDE.md, git status and preloaded skills - never the parent conversation.
findings.implication: Every reviewer/judge is a fresh subagent with a short system prompt plus spec, diff and evidence. Never 'compact and continue' a reviewer; split big diffs so each reviewer's input stays small.

findings.claim: Reviewers must execute, not just read: success claims need evidence artifacts, and subagent summaries are not trustworthy by default.
findings.evidence: Anthropic harness (read): the evaluator 'use[s] the Playwright MCP to click through the running application the way a user would'; sprint contracts fail if any item fails ('FAIL - Tool only places tiles at drag start/end points instead of filling the region'). Effective harnesses (read): testing tools 'dramatically improved performance, as the agent was able to identify and fix bugs that weren't obvious from the code alone'; later agents 'declare the job done' prematurely. Best practices (read): 'Have Claude show evidence rather than asserting success: the test output, the command it ran and what it returned, or a screenshot'; 'If you can't verify it, don't ship it'. /goal doc (read): its evaluator 'doesn't run commands or read files independently'. User-reported (not a study): '20-30% of subagent reports contain at least one claim that doesn't match the underlying tool output' over 200+ sessions.
findings.implication: The author stage must emit an evidence bundle (exact commands, raw outputs, test results, screenshots). Reviewers re-run tests themselves (read-only on source, Bash for test/build). Transcript-only judges are cheap pre-gates, not the outside verdict. Verify subagent claims (counts, file lists) with deterministic checks.

findings.claim: Reviewer independence must be enforced structurally (read-only tools, hooks, required checks defined outside the branch under review), and review depth should be tiered by risk.
findings.evidence: agent-approval-check.yml (read): requires N (default 2) human approvals on PRs containing agent-authored commits (noreply@anthropic.com, claude[bot], claude-code[bot]); 'Both triggers run the workflow file from the BASE/DEFAULT branch, so a PR cannot edit this check to approve itself'; bot approvers excluded; required status check; exempt paths and protected bases configurable. Anthropic SDLC (read): 'multiple gates and agents with separate context windows... They do not share biases and blindspots. If one is compromised or makes a mistake, it can be caught by other reviewers'; 'Tiering our codebase by risk'; 'Every approval is logged with the signals and reasoning behind it, and a risk-weighted sample is reviewed by humans'. Best practices (read): 'Unlike CLAUDE.md instructions which are advisory, hooks are deterministic'. Meta RADAR (2026): gated funnel with deterministic validation landed 331K+ diffs with revert rate 1/3 and incident rate 1/50 of non-RADAR diffs; widening the risk envelope p25 -> p50 raised auto-approve to 60.31% with stable safety.
findings.implication: Define reviewers in .claude/agents with tools restricted to Read/Grep/Glob plus test execution; gate merges with a Stop hook or required check whose definition lives on the base branch; agent approvals never count; route trivial/low-risk diffs past the outside judge and require human approval on high-risk paths (auth, payments, migrations, PII); log every verdict with evidence.

findings.claim: Keep reviewable units small: human inspection data caps effective review at roughly 200-400 lines per session, and understanding the change is the real bottleneck.
findings.evidence: SmartBear/Cisco study: 'review no more than 200 to 400 lines of code... beyond 400 LOC, the ability to find defects diminishes'; '200-400 LOC over 60 to 90 minutes should yield 70-90% defect discovery'. Google case study (Sadowski 2018): median change ~24 lines, ~90% touch <10 files, median 1 approver. Bacchelli & Bird (read): 'Understanding code and changes emerged as the critical bottleneck'; defects are a minority of comments despite being the top expectation. Claude Code Review: cost and time scale with PR size; ultrareview caps at 500 files / 8,000 changed lines.
findings.implication: The decomposition stage should produce units of roughly <=300 changed lines with their own binary acceptance criteria, so each independent review is small (also limits context rot) and 'send back to the beginning' is cheap; big tasks get many small reviews then one integration review.

findings.claim: AI review suggestions are adopted less and are wrong more often than human ones unless aggressively filtered; noisy reviewers get tuned out, so precision must beat recall in what reaches the author.
findings.evidence: Human-AI Synergy in Agentic Code Review (2026): 278,790 review conversations across 300 projects; AI suggestions 'adopted into the codebase at a significantly lower rate'; 'Over half of unadopted suggestions from AI agents are either incorrect or addressed through alternative fixes'; adopted AI suggestions 'produce significantly larger increases in code complexity and code size'. Liang et al. (read): GPT-4 feedback overlaps human reviewers as much as humans overlap each other (30.85% vs 28.58%; 39.23% vs 35.25%) but 'often struggles to provide in-depth critique of method design'. Claude Code REVIEW.md guidance (read): 'Report at most five Nits... say plus N similar items'; 'behavior claims need a file:line citation in the source, not an inference from naming'.
findings.implication: Cap nits, require file:line citations, separate Important / Nit / Pre-existing, and track the thumbs-down rate per reviewer to recalibrate thresholds. Expect LLM judges to be good at 'is this wrong or incomplete' and weak at 'is this the best design'; route design questions to the hypothesis-check stage, not the final judge.
