It gave no onboarding procedure.

Research a 'Day 0 to Day 30' procedure for standing the funnel up on a real legacy repository:
1. Baseline: obtaining a trustworthy green baseline when tests are absent, slow or flaky - characterization tests and seams (Feathers, Working Effectively with Legacy Code), golden-master / approval tests (ApprovalTests, Jest snapshots treated as reviewed artifacts with role-restricted updates), flaky-test hunting and quarantine with a scheduled rerun workflow, the 'init.sh + smoke test + baseline commit' ritual from Anthropic's long-running harness, and what to do when the build cannot be reproduced (containerize first; the SWE-bench FAIL_TO_PASS / PASS_TO_PASS criterion as the gate).
2. Zones of responsibility from evidence: deriving the path map from git history (co-change coupling, hotspots, knowledge maps per Tornhill), module boundaries, and the known overlap zones (auth/authz, config, migrations, shared helpers, API contracts, core services); validating the map by logging agent write-set conflicts; keeping it small enough to load every session; representing it as CODEOWNERS plus path-scoped .claude/rules.
3. Codebase knowledge for agents without bloating context: repository maps (Aider repo-map, tree-sitter symbol indexes), Claude Code code-intelligence plugins / LSP, ctags, semantic code search; how to enforce 'confirm with code search before assuming functionality is missing' as a hook or a mandatory research subagent; what /init and /doctor produce; deriving a <200-line CLAUDE.md plus path-scoped rules from README, CI config, lint configs and ADRs; when a skill is the right home instead.
4. Safe landing on a live system: feature flags and branch-by-abstraction for the walking skeleton, strangler-fig for rewrites, migrations under change control, stacked slices, diff-scoped quality gates, and how to size units when surrounding code is untested (characterize first, then change).
5. Monorepo / multi-service / multi-language specifics: per-package .claude/ directories and workflows closest to the working directory, cross-repo contracts (Pact can-i-deploy), generated and vendored directories to exclude from review and from write permissions, mixed-tool fleets (pin one tool and formatter config per repo given cross-agent conflict rates).
6. Legacy-specific agent failure modes with a mechanical countermeasure for each: duplicating existing helpers, breaking implicit invariants, 'fixing' flaky tests by weakening them, editing generated files or migrations, retro-documenting instead of changing, touching files outside the zone (PreToolUse path denies, append-only test paths, forbidden-path lists in briefs).
7. Measuring the onboarding: what to record in the first 30 days (rework, agent conflicts per zone, characterization tests added, escaped defects, time-to-green) and how to compare against METR-style expectations for mature codebases.

Deliver: a phased onboarding checklist with concrete commands and tools per ecosystem (JS/TS, Python, Go, Java/Kotlin, Rust, PHP at minimum); a zones-map derivation recipe; a CLAUDE.md and .claude/rules starter template; the hook and path-deny list; and an evidence level per recommendation, noting explicitly where a practice is human-era and its transfer to agents is unmeasured. Use primary sources; mark blocked ones.

weak_claims: Stop-hook block cap: D6 says 'the hooks reference says three, the hooks guide says eight'. The hooks guide (fetched 2026-09-26) says Claude Code overrides a Stop hook 'after it blocks eight times in a row without progress', configurable via CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_BLOCK_CAP; no 'three' was found. The sweep also omits that the cap is progress-sensitive, which changes how a 'block until green' gate should be designed.

'Independent review must run in a fresh context that sees only the diff and the criteria' (D1/D3/D7, marked high) is contradicted by Anthropic's own recipe in the same best-practices page, which hands the reviewer PLAN.md and lets it fetch repository context, and by D7's proposal of a blind tier with 'no plan'. The sweep never settles whether the plan/spec is allowed, and its own working assumption (spec allowed, transcript not) is asserted without evidence.

'Reviewer independence enforced structurally via read-only tools' (D3/D7) conflicts with 'reviewers must execute, not just read' (D3): a subagent tools allowlist that includes Bash can still write files, so 'read-only' is not achieved by tool lists alone; the reconciliation (Bash only inside isolation: worktree or a container, with a PreToolUse hook) is missing.

'The author must never be allowed to argue with the reviewer' (D3, high) is not reconciled with the reference pattern the sweep also endorses, in which review findings are returned to the implementing session, which decides what to fix and re-reviews. Where adjudication happens is unspecified.

'Additional review rounds on the same artifact lower precision sharply' (F1 0.376 -> 0.26-0.30, from a blocked arXiv paper) is presented alongside 'converge on re-review' and 'approvals expire on new commits' without distinguishing re-review of an unchanged version from review of a changed one; the numbers themselves were not verified.

The Cross-Context Review F1 figures (self-review 24.6%, context-aware subagent 23.8%, cold reviewer 28.6%, on 30 small artifacts) are small differences from a single unverified source, yet 'independence = separate context' is rated high in three dimensions largely on this basis; effect size and significance are unknown.

'Multi-agent systems cost ~15x a chat's tokens' comes from Anthropic's research system and is reused as a coding cost across dimensions, while D4 separately cites '3-10x a single agent'; no coding-specific measurement exists. The only concrete coding numbers are ultrareview's $5-25 and 5-10 minutes.

'<1% of findings marked incorrect' and 'substantive-comment rate 16% -> 54%' are vendor thumbs-down rates on Anthropic's own PRs, not precision/recall; the sweep flags this in one open question but cites the figures as high-confidence evidence elsewhere.

'Split work by ownership, never by discipline or phase' (D4, high) is in tension with the funnel itself, which is phase-split (plan -> implement -> review) and with D2's spec -> plan -> tasks pipeline; the reconciliation (phase-split is fine for a sequential single item, ownership-split is required only for parallel writers) is never stated.

'Codify the orchestration as a workflow script: the script holds the plan and intermediate results, is resumable and deterministic' (D1/D2/D8) overstates persistence: the docs state the script has no filesystem or shell access, results live in script variables, resume works only within the same session (or its --resume), and a failed agent reruns every agent started after it. Durable funnel state must be written by agents to disk; the sweep never says so.

'Claude Code's shared task list natively blocks tasks with unresolved dependencies with file-locked claiming' (D4, high) is true but describes agent teams, which the docs mark experimental, disabled by default, interactive-only (no -p / SDK), non-nesting, with lagging task status and no session resume; presenting it as a ready primitive for the funnel's backbone is misleading.

'A PreToolUse deny cannot be overridden even in bypassPermissions mode' (D8, high) could not be confirmed in the hooks reference or guide fetched today; treat as unverified until tested on the installed version.

'Subagents are the wrong tool for iterative back-and-forth' (D1) is partially outdated: current docs allow named subagents to be messaged and resumed (SendMessage), so the constraint is weaker than stated, though fresh-context review still argues against reuse.

AI-agent merge-conflict rates (27.67% overall; 41.7% vs 19.8% cross- vs same-agent pairs; ~10% at 2 lines to ~30% at 25 lines) come from arXiv 2607.04697, which was blocked; the numbers are unverified and the causal story (style divergence) is admitted guesswork.

'Roughly one in five package recommendations is hallucinated' is from a 2024 study on older models; the claim that agents 'invent packages at a measurable rate even on frontier models' rests on a blocked 2026 summary covering releases only to March 2026. Rates for current models are unknown.

'Security defects in ~45% of AI-generated code, not improving across generations' is a single vendor report (Veracode) rated low; it should not drive a mandatory security tier without independent support.

'TDD yields 40-90% lower pre-release defect density at 15-35% time cost' is Nagappan et al. 2008 on four human teams; transfer to AI agents (where the implementer must be barred from editing tests) is unmeasured, yet D8 presents it as evidence for test-first in an AI pipeline.

The scope-sentence effect (overeager rate 0.0% -> 17.1% when the sentence is removed; 5-28% overeager rates) is from a single unreplicated preprint; the mitigation is cheap but the magnitude should not be quoted as established.

Several LLM-judge figures (style-not-length bias, 9 judges from 7 families = ~2 effective votes, 13.6% pairwise flip rate, '80+ agents unanimously endorsed a non-existent vulnerability', 11-15 trials for pairwise judgments) cite arXiv IDs that were blocked or carry 2605/2606 numbering; none was read in full and they should not be quoted in a deliverable without verification.

'Human review is effective at ~200-400 lines per session' (SmartBear/Cisco 2006 human inspection data) is applied to AI reviewers with no evidence, and sits beside ultrareview's 8,000-changed-line acceptance; there is no reconciled diff budget for AI-authored, AI-reviewed units (D4 says 100-400, D7 says ~100, D8 cites 1000 as 'too large').

Loop caps are inconsistent and none is empirically derived: 2 failed corrections (Claude Code), 3 strikes (superpowers debugging), rounds 1-3 same implementer / 4-5 stronger model (superpowers SDD), 5 repair iterations (BMAD), 8 Stop-hook blocks (Claude Code). The sweep presents each as high-confidence without noting they cannot all be the rule.

'Separate the evaluator from the generator' (D1, high) vs 'Anthropic stripped the per-sprint evaluator after Opus 4.6' (D3 open question) and 'only pay for an evaluator when the task exceeds what the model does reliably solo' (D1): the sweep does not say when a separate evaluator is worth it on current models, so the funnel's review tiers rest on a claim its own sources qualify.

'Default-heavy when in doubt' (superpowers brainstorming) and 'skip the plan for one-sentence diffs' (Claude Code) are both cited as high-confidence guidance in D2/D5; they are contradictory defaults with no comparative measurement.

Sycophancy evidence ('models abandon correct answers when challenged') is from 2023 studies on older models; the magnitude for current Claude models is unknown, so the design rule may be right but its cited support is dated.

'AGENTS.md convention: listed test commands are run automatically' (D2) is a statement about some tools' conventions from the agents.md FAQ, not Claude Code behavior; it should not be relied on as an enforcement mechanism.

All quantitative SDD gains (Mercari 1.6x / 150%, Ralph $297, Kitchen Loop zero regressions, ~50% fewer errors with human-refined specs) are self-reported; Thoughtworks rates SDD 'Assess'; the sweep's own D2 says this, but D1/D8 cite spec-first as high-confidence acceleration.

METR's 19% slowdown is for early-2025 tools (Cursor with Claude 3.5/3.7) on mature repos; METR has since changed its design; it is evidence that acceleration must be measured, not evidence about structured agentic funnels either way.

D7's classics (Reason's Swiss cheese, Haynes 2009 checklist, Klein's premortem, Degani & Wiener, DORA change-approval, Ontario checklist 'no effect without culture change') were not fetched and are quoted from memory at medium confidence; the 'checklists ticked by the doer do not work' claim in particular needs a primary source before it shapes the design.

The '60-70% context fill dumb zone' threshold is folklore per D6's own note; Chroma's data suggests smooth, distractor-sensitive degradation, so any stage-sizing rule keyed to a fill percentage is unsupported.

'Set-based design: spawn 2-3 parallel spikes and let evidence eliminate them' is supported by Toyota automotive engineering and practitioner anecdote only; no controlled coding comparison exists, and it is the mechanism the sweep credits with turning the straight line into a funnel.

'Run co-change analysis before drawing zones' (D4, high) is a plausible heuristic backed by a tool's existence (code-maat), not by evidence that it reduces agent write conflicts; it should be rated medium and validated by logging conflicts per zone.

'Grade the end state, not the path' (D1/D7/D8, high) sits uneasily with the funnel's many process constraints (sterile cockpit, checklists at pause points, mandatory RED run, hooks that constrain tool sequences); the sweep does not say which process rules are gates and which are merely advisory, so a designer could grade process by accident.

value.dimension: Separator calibration: risk/size routing, per-tier cost/latency/model budgets, and measuring whether the funnel actually accelerates work

findings.claim: Change size is the best-evidenced pre-implementation risk signal; route <=~50 lines / <=2 files to the light path and treat >300 lines or >8 files as heavy by default.
findings.evidence: Google eng-practices: '100 lines is usually a reasonable size for a CL, and 1000 lines is usually too large'; small CLs are 'Less likely to introduce bugs' and 'Simpler to roll back'. Anthropic Code Review post (vendor): PRs <50 lines get findings 31% of the time (0.5 avg) vs 84% (7.5 avg) for >1,000 lines, at $15-25 and ~20 min per review. Bosu et al. (Microsoft, 1.5M comments): 'the more files that are in a change, the lower the proportion of comments ... that will be of value'. Nagappan & Ball: relative churn predicts defect density with 89.0% accuracy on Windows Server 2003.
findings.implication: Size bands are the backbone of the router; the heavy review layers have ~0.5 expected findings on small diffs, so applying them uniformly is the most expensive mistake.

findings.claim: Overlap zones (shared helpers, core services, auth, contracts) should be a deterministic path-to-zone map with hard tier floors, because dependency-graph centrality predicts defects better than code complexity.
findings.evidence: Zimmermann & Nagappan (ICSE 2008): network measures 'could identify 60% of the binaries that the Windows developers considered as critical - twice as many as identified by complexity metrics'; recall '10% points higher than for models built from complexity metrics'. Anthropic SDLC post: 'Tiering our codebase by risk and then automating reviews based on that level.'
findings.implication: Zone contact is computed from git paths, not by an LLM; migrations => heavy floor, auth/deps/contracts => at least medium floor; any zone touched by an actual diff triggers promotion.

findings.claim: Low-ownership contributions correlate with failures at least as strongly as size, churn or complexity, so 'no prior landed change in this module' is a legitimate +risk signal, though the agent analogy is unproven.
findings.evidence: Bird et al. 2011 Table 1 (read from the PDF): Spearman correlation with pre/post-release failures - Minor contributors 0.86/0.70 (Vista), 0.93/0.25 (Win7); Size 0.75/0.69; Churn 0.72/0.69; Complexity 0.70/0.53; abstract: 'the removal of low-expertise contributions dramatically decreases the performance of contribution based defect prediction'. (A WebFetch summary reported '0.52' and '25-30%'; the 0.52 is wrong per Table 1 and the 25-30% figure was not found in the text.)
findings.implication: Track landed tasks per path in telemetry and add +1 for novel areas; validate the analogy on your own escape data before weighting it higher.

findings.claim: There is no universal defect-predictor weight set; router weights must be a prior that is re-fit from the repo's own telemetry.
findings.evidence: Nagappan, Ball, Zeller (ICSE 2006): 'There is no single set of complexity metrics that could act as a universally best defect predictor'; predictors built from a project's own history, though 'predictors obtained from one project can also be significant for new, similar projects'.
findings.implication: Ship the rubric (size, files, modules, zones, co-change, churn, novelty, tests, contract, ambiguity; floors for migrations/auth/deps) as a starting point and fit a logistic model of send-back-or-escape on raw signals after ~50 logged tasks.

findings.claim: The router should be deterministic-first with a schema-constrained Haiku classifier only for signals git cannot see, and every decision logged with its signals.
findings.evidence: Anthropic SDLC: 'Every automated approval, tool call, and agent-to-agent message is logged with the signals it used and lands in our SIEM'; 'A risk-weighted sample is reviewed by humans.' Meta RADAR (arXiv 2605.30208, blocked; via prior researcher's notes): funnel = eligibility gates -> static heuristics -> ML risk score -> LLM review; revert rate 1/3 and incident rate 1/50 of non-RADAR diffs; relaxing threshold p25->p50 raised approve rate to 60.31% with stable safety. Claude Code workflows enforce JSON schemas on agent() output with up to 5 validation attempts (MAX_STRUCTURED_OUTPUT_RETRIES).
findings.implication: Implement the scorer as a hook/skill script over git + the intake artifact writing router.jsonl; call agent(prompt,{model:'haiku',effort:'low',schema}) only for predicted files/lines, ambiguity, reversibility; classifier output never lowers a floor.

findings.claim: Vendor guidance already defines the light path and the promotion trigger: skip planning for one-sentence diffs, and treat two failed corrections as the signal to restart with more structure.
findings.evidence: Claude Code best practices: 'If you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan'; 'Planning is most useful when you're uncertain about the approach, when the change modifies multiple files, or when you're unfamiliar with the code'; failure pattern fix: 'After two failed corrections, /clear and write a better initial prompt incorporating what you learned.'
findings.implication: LIGHT = implement + deterministic hook gate + one cheap fresh-context reviewer; promotion rule = 2 failed gate/review cycles OR zone contact OR >2x predicted size, restarting at the higher path's plan stage with evidence but not the failed transcript.

findings.claim: Claude Code provides a four-rung verification ladder whose deterministic rungs (Stop hook, up to 10 consecutive blocks) and fresh-context rung (refuting subagent/workflow) map directly onto the funnel's gates and send-backs.
findings.evidence: Best practices: 'In one prompt ... Across a session: /goal ... As a deterministic gate: a Stop hook runs your check as a script and blocks the turn from ending until it passes ... By a second opinion: a verification subagent or a dynamic workflow ... has a fresh model try to refute the result, so the agent doing the work isn't the one grading it.' Hooks reference: Stop input includes stop_hook_active and consecutive_blocks; a Stop hook can block at most 10 times consecutively; SubagentStop provides agent_id, agent_type, last_assistant_message but no subagent transcript path; subagent frontmatter hooks run only while that subagent runs.
findings.implication: Gate = Stop/PostToolUse hook running tests; verdict capture = parse JSON from SubagentStop last_assistant_message; token counts must come from OTel or transcripts, not from the hook payload.

findings.claim: Token economics differ sharply by mechanism: subagents summarize back (cheapest), workflows keep results out of context and cap at 16 concurrent agents with a Large-workflow warning above 25 agents or 1.5M projected tokens, and agent teams cost ~7x a normal session.
findings.evidence: Agent teams doc table: 'Token cost - Subagents: Lower: results summarized back ... Agent teams: Higher: each teammate is a separate Claude instance'; costs doc: 'Agent teams use approximately 7x more tokens than standard sessions when teammates run in plan mode'. Workflows doc: 'Up to 16 concurrent agents by default, fewer when Claude Code has fewer CPUs'; '1,000 agents total per run'; 'When a workflow schedules more than 25 agents, or its projected token total passes 1.5 million ... shows a Large workflow warning'; workflowSizeGuideline small <5 / medium <10 / large <50, default medium (small on Pro). Subagent limit: 20 concurrent (CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS), depth 3; both lifted under ultracode.
findings.implication: Use workflows for the heavy path's fan-outs (pipeline, schema, budget), subagents for light/medium, and avoid agent teams except for genuinely parallel investigations; note the prior '16-concurrent default' applies to workflow agents, not to Agent-tool subagents (20).

findings.claim: Prompt-cache rules decide fan-out cost: subagents/workflow agents get a 5-minute TTL even on subscriptions, siblings share a prefix only if model/effort/agentType/tools/schema/cwd match and start after the first response begins (5 s stagger), and 1-hour TTL costs 2x on writes.
findings.evidence: Workflows doc: 'Two agents that run with the same model, effort level, agent type, tools, output schema, and working directory build the same tools-and-system-prompt prefix ... Claude Code holds all but the first until the first agent's response begins ... caps the hold at CLAUDE_CODE_WORKFLOW_PREFIX_STAGGER_MS ... 5000 by default'; 'its cache holds for five minutes by default, including on a Claude subscription. To keep it for an hour, set subagentPromptCacheTtl to 1h.' Platform pricing: 5-minute writes 1.25x, 1-hour writes 2x, reads 0.1x (Fable 5.1 0.025x, Opus 5.5 0.05x); 'a cache entry only becomes available after the first response begins'. Claude Code caching doc: each model and (on most models) each effort level has its own cache; switching mid-session re-reads the whole history.
findings.implication: Define lens reviewers as ONE agent type with the lens in the prompt; set subagentPromptCacheTtl=1h when send-back loops exceed 5 minutes; never change the implementer's model/effort mid-task.

findings.claim: Model-per-stage is controllable with a documented precedence order, and list prices (cached 2026-06-24) make Haiku triage ~10x cheaper than Opus and Fable 5.1 2x Opus 5.
findings.evidence: Sub-agents doc precedence: '1. The per-invocation model parameter 2. The subagent definition's model frontmatter ... 3. CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL ... 4. The main conversation's model'; CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL_FORCE=1 overrides all (v2.1.257+). claude-api skill price table: Haiku 4.5 $1/$5, Sonnet 5 $2/$10, Opus 5 $5/$25, Opus 5.5 $4/$20 (launching), Fable 5.1 $10/$50 per MTok. model-config: effort levels low/medium/high/xhigh/max; defaults Opus 5.5 medium, Opus 4.7 xhigh, others high; workflow agent() accepts model and effort per call.
findings.source: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents ; https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config ; bundled claude-api skill (Current Models table, cached 2026-06-24)
findings.implication: Haiku/low for routing, schema extraction and plan checks; Sonnet 5/high for implementation and lens reviewers; Opus 5/xhigh for decomposition, judge panels and the blind verdict; Fable 5.1 only for the blind verdict on heavy tasks if seeded-defect calibration shows a catch-rate gain worth 2x.

findings.claim: Estimated cost/latency per path (assumptions stated in the notes): LIGHT $0.5-1.2 and 5-15 min; MEDIUM $4.5-9 (Sonnet impl) to $9-16 (Opus impl) and 25-55 min with 2-5 human minutes; HEAVY $25-45 to $45-90 plus optional $5-25 ultrareview, 60-150 min with 20-40 human minutes.
findings.evidence: Anchors: Anthropic harness post 'The harness was over 20x more expensive' ($9 solo vs $200 full harness) and 'It is worth the cost when the task sits beyond what the current model does reliably solo'; multi-agent research post 'multi-agent systems use about 15x more tokens than chats'; managed Code Review '$15-25 ... completing in 20 minutes on average'; ultrareview 'typically $5 to $25', '5 to 10 minutes', '500 changed files and 8,000 changed lines'; enterprise average '$13 per developer per active day ... below $30 per active day for 90% of users'. Table assumes 25-40k uncached prefix per agent, 85-92% cache hit, list prices above.
findings.implication: The heavy/light ratio (~30-70x) means routing accuracy dominates total spend; treat the table as a placeholder to be overwritten by measured cost_usd/duration_ms after the first 10 runs per path.

findings.claim: Hard budget enforcement exists today at three levels (query spend cap, subagent concurrency/depth, workflow token budget) and should bound every stage rather than relying on advisory warnings.
findings.evidence: Agent SDK subagents doc: maxBudgetUsd/max_budget_usd 'refuses to spawn more subagents, returning Budget limit reached, stops background subagents that are still running, and ends the query with the error_max_budget_usd result subtype'; CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS default 20; CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH default 3. workflow-authoring skill: budget.total is 'a HARD ceiling, not advisory: once spent() reaches total, further agent() calls throw'; maxTurns marks output partial and is resumable.
findings.implication: Give each path a cap (e.g. light $2, medium $15, heavy $90) via --max-budget-usd / budget.total; a cap hit is a logged stop-and-escalate event, not a silent truncation.

findings.claim: Telemetry can be captured today from four documented sources, with three gotchas: OTel redacts custom agent names unless OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1, the SDK 'usage' field excludes subagents (use total_cost_usd/modelUsage), and transcripts are deleted after 30 days.
findings.evidence: Monitoring doc: claude_code.api_request carries model, cost_usd, duration_ms, input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_read_tokens, cache_creation_tokens, effort, agent.name, prompt.id, workflow.run_id; tool_result carries tool_name, success, duration_ms, result_tokens; cost/token metrics carry query_source main|subagent|auxiliary; 'user-defined agent names are replaced with "custom" unless OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1'. Cost-tracking doc: 'usage: Excluded [subagent activity] ... total_cost_usd: Included ... modelUsage: Included'; 'Per-step output_tokens is a placeholder'. Claude directory: transcripts at ~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session>.jsonl and <session>/subagents/, cleanupPeriodDays default 30. Workflows: every run writes journal.jsonl recording each agent's return value.
findings.implication: Schema per stage: task_id, path, route_changes, stage, attempt, run_id, agent_id/type, model, effort, tokens x4, cost_usd, wall_ms, gate result, verdict, findings{reported,confirmed,refuted,unverified}, send_backs, human minutes, diff stats, commit_hash, regime_id; capture via hooks->JSONL + OTel console/OTLP + claude -p --output-format json + nightly export of transcripts/journals + git notes.

findings.claim: Lines, commits, throughput and self-report are invalid acceleration metrics; AI adoption raises volume while lowering stability and refactoring share.
findings.evidence: DORA 2024: 'As AI adoption increased, it was accompanied by an estimated decrease in delivery throughput by 1.5%, and an estimated reduction in delivery stability by 7.2%' (per 25% adoption increase). DORA 2025: 90% use AI; positive relationship with throughput, but 'AI adoption does continue to have a negative relationship with software delivery stability'; 'AI doesn't fix a team; it amplifies what's already there.' GitClear 2025 PDF (211M lines): moved/refactored lines fell from 24.1% (2020) to 9.5% (2024); copy/paste and 2-week churn rose. METR 2025 RCT (metr.org blocked; via prior notes): 16 developers, 246 tasks, 19% slower while believing +20%.
findings.implication: Prove acceleration with time-to-land, rework rate (send-backs/landed + 14-day churn), defect escape rate, cost per landed change and human minutes per landed change on matched tasks; never with output volume or how fast it felt.

findings.claim: pass^k (all k trials succeed) is the right consistency metric for gates and eval sets, and it decays fast: on tau-bench retail pass^1 0.692 -> pass^4 0.462 for the same model.
findings.evidence: Anthropic evals post: 'pass@k measures the likelihood that an agent gets at least one correct solution in k attempts' while 'pass^k measures the probability that all k trials succeed'. tau-bench README leaderboard (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, tool-calling): retail Pass^1 0.692, Pass^2 0.576, Pass^3 0.509, Pass^4 0.462; airline 0.460 -> 0.225.
findings.implication: Run the failure eval set and seeded-defect set at k=3 per path and report pass^3; a gate whose pass^3 is far below its pass@1 is flaky, not protective.

findings.claim: The calibration protocol should start from 20-50 real failures, grade each dimension with an isolated judge that may answer 'Unknown', and read transcripts; evals are what make model swaps re-validatable in days.
findings.evidence: Anthropic evals post: '20-50 simple tasks drawn from real failures is a great start'; 'give the LLM a way out, like providing an instruction to return Unknown'; 'grade each dimension with an isolated LLM-as-judge rather than using one to grade all dimensions'; 'You won't know if your graders are working well unless you read the transcripts and grades from many trials'; teams with evals 'can quickly determine the model's strengths, tune their prompts, and upgrade in days'.
findings.implication: Build the eval set from ~/.claude/projects transcripts and git history before they age out; seed one known defect per diff per class; measure catch rate, precision and cost per reviewer layer at k=3; re-run on every model/effort/version change (regime id in telemetry).

findings.claim: Review layers must have an expiry: strip components one at a time as models improve, keeping only those whose seeded-defect catch rate stays above zero.
findings.evidence: Anthropic harness-design post: 'I moved to a more methodical approach, removing one component at a time and reviewing what impact it had on the final result'; 'The evaluator is still an LLM that is inclined to be generous towards LLM-generated outputs'. Anthropic harness-patterns post: 'Agent harnesses encode assumptions about what Claude can't do on its own. As Claude gets more capable, those assumptions should be tested.' (prior researcher's read of the same post: 'When a new model lands, it is generally good practice to re-examine a harness, stripping away pieces that are no longer load-bearing.')
findings.implication: Retirement rule: a layer with 0 unique confirmed catches and precision <50% over 30 runs (>=20 seeded, >=10 real) is disabled; remove one layer at a time and re-run the seeded set; evaluators need a prosecutorial mandate and binary contracts.

findings.claim: Reviewer findings are not a value metric: reviewers over-report by construction, so only refuter-confirmed findings count, and 'unverified' must be a first-class verdict.
findings.evidence: Claude Code best practices: 'A reviewer prompted to find gaps will usually report some, even when the work is sound ... Tell the reviewer to flag only gaps that affect correctness or the stated requirements'. Workflows doc (/deep-research): 'When the verifier agents can't check a claim ... the report lists that claim as unverified instead of counting it as refuted'. Czerwonka et al. abstract: 'code reviews often do not find functionality issues that should block a code submission'. Code Review docs: verification step 'checks candidates against actual code behavior to filter out false positives'.
findings.implication: Per-layer metrics are catch rate (unique confirmed / all confirmed + escapes), precision (confirmed / reported), unverified fraction and cost per confirmed finding; send-backs are triggered only by confirmed findings.

findings.claim: The blind verdict and the reviewers must run in fresh contexts that see only a style-stripped bundle (spec, diff, test evidence), because a session is biased toward code it just wrote and separate contexts do not share blind spots.
findings.evidence: Best practices: 'A fresh context improves code review since Claude won't be biased toward code it just wrote' (Writer/Reviewer pattern); 'A reviewer running in a fresh subagent context sees only the diff and the criteria you give it, not the reasoning that produced the change'. Anthropic SDLC: reviewers with separate context windows 'do not share biases and blindspots. If one is compromised or makes a mistake, it can be caught by other reviewers.' Sub-agents doc: 'Each subagent starts with a fresh, isolated context window.'
findings.implication: The heavy path's context-free judge is a non-fork subagent or workflow agent (never a fork) fed spec + diff + evidence only, with no dialogue channel back to the implementer; a FAIL routes to decomposition, not to a fix cycle.

anti_patterns: Applying the full funnel to every task: <50-line PRs yield findings 31% of the time (0.5 avg) at $15-25 and ~20 min; the full harness costs ~20x solo ($9 -> $200); Claude Code's own guidance is 'If you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan'.

Routing with an LLM alone and not logging the decision: Meta RADAR and Anthropic's SDLC put deterministic gates/heuristics before ML/LLM and log every approval with the signals used; an unlogged classifier cannot be calibrated and a classifier must never lower a hard floor (migrations, auth, dependencies).

Using one universal weight set for risk: Nagappan/Ball/Zeller found 'no single set of complexity metrics that could act as a universally best defect predictor'; weights must be re-fit per repository from telemetry.

Measuring acceleration by lines, commits, throughput or self-report: DORA 2024 (-1.5% throughput, -7.2% stability per 25% AI adoption), DORA 2025 (stability still negative), GitClear (refactoring share 24.1% -> 9.5%, churn up), METR (19% slower while believing +20%; source blocked).

Counting reviewer findings as value: reviewers 'will usually report some [gaps], even when the work is sound'; comment usefulness falls with change size; count only refuter-confirmed findings and track precision per layer.

Letting the implementing session (or a fork of it) act as reviewer or judge: fresh contexts are required because a session is biased toward code it just wrote and LLM evaluators are 'inclined to be generous'.
Using agent teams for sequential or same-file work: ~7x tokens in plan mode, coordination overhead, and teammate plans are auto-approved by the lead 'without the lead reviewing it'.

Designing fan-outs that defeat the cache: reviewers with different model/effort/agentType/tools/schema share no prefix; subagents get a 5-minute TTL by default even on subscriptions; changing model or effort mid-session re-reads the whole history; opusplan restarts the cache on every plan toggle.
Reading the SDK/CLI 'usage' field as total spend (it excludes subagents; use total_cost_usd or modelUsage) and trusting per-step output_tokens (a placeholder).

Relying on OTel agent.name for stage attribution without OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1 (custom agent names are redacted to 'custom'), or on ~/.claude/projects transcripts as the telemetry store (deleted after cleanupPeriodDays, 30 by default).
Keeping every review layer forever: strip components one at a time as models improve; a layer whose seeded-defect catch rate stays ~0 is pure latency and cost.
Letting promote/demote rules flip-flop: demotion only at the plan stage and only once per task; two promotions => human decides.

Assuming '16 concurrent agents' everywhere: 16 is the workflow runtime cap (min(16, CPUs-2)); Agent-tool subagents cap at 20; both limits are lifted under ultracode, which also suppresses the Large-workflow warning.
open_questions: Which of the 14 pre-implementation signals actually predict defects in AI-authored changes: every cited defect-prediction study is about human-authored code, and the rubric weights are only a prior until ~50 tasks are logged per repository.
Does 'agent has never landed a change in this module' behave like Bird et al.'s minor-contributor effect (Spearman 0.86/0.70 with failures)? No direct evidence exists.
Does test coverage of the target area predict escapes for AI changes? The human-code literature (Mockus 2009, Kochhar 2017) is weak/mixed and could not be re-verified (hosts blocked).
Kamei et al. JIT numbers (68% accuracy, 64% recall, 35% of defect-inducing changes with 20% of effort) are from memory; every mirror was egress-blocked.

Meta RADAR figures (revert 1/3, incidents 1/50, p25->p50 threshold -> 60.31% approve rate) come from another researcher's search snippets; arXiv was blocked, so the paper's exact design is unverified.
METR 2025 numbers (16 devs, 246 tasks, 19% slower, +24% forecast, +20% belief) are search-level via prior notes; metr.org is blocked and METR announced a 2026 design update that could not be read.
My two fetched summaries of the hooks and agent-teams pages disagree on whether exit code 2 on TaskCompleted blocks completion; verify before using it as a quality gate.
Whether Fable 5.1 as the blind judge improves catch rate enough to justify 2x Opus 5 pricing; only the seeded-defect calibration can answer it.
How to attribute post-land escapes to a specific change reliably in a solo repo without a bug tracker (git blame/bisect automation is a design, not a verified tool).

Ultrareview's fleet size and per-finding precision are not published; Tornhill 'Code Red' (2x time, 15x defects), Shin et al. vulnerability recall, SmartBear 200-400 LOC and Google's median 24-line CL were all blocked and are cited from memory or prior notes only.
The per-path cost/latency table is an estimate from list prices and assumed cache hit rates (85-92%); the first 10 measured runs per path must replace it.

value.dimension: The wide mouth: turning a vague, compound vibe-coder prompt into routed, sized, gradeable work items

findings.claim: Type every ask into one of seven classes (bug, feature, refactor, chore, question, idea, improve) and route by type; shipped tools already do this with closed enums and separate paths.
findings.evidence: Spec Kit's assess-intake command writes a `Type` field with the enum `new-capability | improvement | fix | exploration | cost-saving | compliance | other` and its bug extension is a separate assess->fix->test family stored under `.specify/bugs/<slug>/`. Anthropic's 'Building effective agents' defines routing as a workflow that "classifies an input and directs it to a specialized followup task" for "complex tasks where there are distinct categories that are better handled separately." Conventional Commits fixes the vocabulary fix/feat plus build, chore, ci, docs, style, refactor, perf, test. (vendor doc / vendor eng)
findings.implication: The intake artifact's first field is `type`; every other field's requiredness is conditional on it (bug requires a reproduction command, question requires no artifact, idea/improve routes to assess/spike, chore with a one-sentence diff bypasses planning).

findings.claim: Bugs must enter the funnel through a recorded reproduction (RED run) before any fix; an unperformed reproduction is reported as partial/not-run, never verified.
findings.evidence: Claude Code best practices bug prompt: "write a failing test that reproduces the issue, then fix it"; common-workflows tip: "Tell Claude the command to reproduce the issue and get a stack trace". Spec Kit bug extension README: "a reproduction that was not actually performed is reported as `partial` or `not-run`, not `verified`" and the fix "stays within the files listed in the assessment"; bug-assess: "Never invent reproduction steps unsupported by evidence". Superpowers systematic-debugging: "NO FIXES WITHOUT ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION FIRST", "If not reproducible -> gather more data, don't guess", failing test "MUST have before fixing"; verification-before-completion: bug resolved = "Original symptom no longer reproduces", regression test valid = "Red-green cycle confirmed". (vendor doc / practitioner)
findings.implication: Add `reproduction: {cmd, status: verified|partial|not-run, observed}` to bug items and gate implementation on `status == verified` with a PreToolUse hook; the blind verdict later re-runs the same command expecting GREEN.

findings.claim: Questions and one-sentence chores should not enter the funnel at all; planning ceremony is only worth it when scope is uncertain, multi-file, or unfamiliar.
findings.evidence: Claude Code best practices: "For tasks where the scope is clear and the fix is small (like fixing a typo, adding a log line, or renaming a variable) ask Claude to do it directly ... If you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan."; "Planning is most useful when you're uncertain about the approach, when the change modifies multiple files, or when you're unfamiliar with the code being modified."; codebase questions need "No special prompting required" and `/btw` answers "never enter conversation history". BMAD: "One small story or bug can go straight to Build without ticketing" and a light path when the plan is "clean on all three" (intent gaps, irreversible actions, footprint). (vendor doc / practitioner)
findings.implication: Routes `none` (question) and `direct` (chore with a check) exist so the funnel accelerates rather than adds ceremony; the router's cheapest exits are decided at intake from `type` and a one-sentence-diff test.

findings.claim: Search the codebase and the backlog before assuming functionality is missing, and record the queries and hits in the artifact, not a checkbox.
findings.evidence: Exact-phrase code search finds "Search the codebase before assuming functionality is missing" in Ralph-family prompts (crabbuild/crab AGENTS.md, tradestreamhq PROMPT_plan.md "VERIFY FIRST", NoamHadad12 AGENTS.md: "Search the repository before assuming functionality is missing. Implement only that story and its tests. Record unrelated discoveries in the plan instead of expanding scope."); ralph-orchestrator lists "Assuming functionality is missing without code verification" as an anti-pattern. Spec Kit bug-assess: "Search the codebase for suspect files/functions; cite evidence", "Never guess at file paths". Superpowers brainstorming: "Explore the current structure before proposing changes." GitHub MCP server instructions: "Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates." Anthropic multi-agent: "Without detailed task descriptions, agents duplicate work, leave gaps". (practitioner / vendor doc; no controlled measurement)
findings.implication: Schema fields `existing_code_check {queries, hits, verdict: exists|partial|missing}` and `backlog_check {queries, duplicates}` are mandatory and non-empty before the first human question; a `feature` item whose verdict is `exists` is a duplicate and is rejected.

findings.claim: Two work items that touch the same files must be serialized; only items on disjoint files with no dependencies may run in parallel.
findings.evidence: Spec Kit tasks template: task format `[ID] [P?] [Story] Description` where `[P]` means "different files, no dependencies" and tasks touching identical files run sequentially; a Foundational phase blocks all story work. Claude Code agent teams: "Two teammates editing the same file leads to overwrites. Break the work so each teammate owns a different set of files."; worktrees exist "so concurrent edits don't collide". (vendor doc)
findings.implication: Each item carries `authorized_scope.allow_paths`; the intake computes pairwise overlap and sets `shares_files_with` / `parallelizable`, so the distributor never has to ask and can use worktree isolation for the rest.

findings.claim: The standard for a gradeable acceptance criterion is that two independent experts reach the same pass/fail verdict, and everything the grader checks must be visible in the task text.
findings.evidence: Anthropic, 'Demystifying evals for AI agents': "A good task is one where two domain experts would independently reach the same pass/fail verdict." and "Everything the grader checks should be clear from the task description; agents shouldn't fail due to ambiguous specs." Grader table: code-based graders use "Binary tests (fail-to-pass, pass-to-pass)" and are "Objective", "Reproducible"; model-based graders are "Non-deterministic" and need "Calibration with human graders". (vendor eng)
findings.implication: Intake release gate: run a two-grader dry run (two fresh small-model subagents given each AC plus a synthetic pass and a synthetic fail) and reword any AC where they disagree; the context-free verdict agent grades only against this pre-agreed text.

findings.claim: Decomposing evaluation into instruction-specific YES/NO checklist items measurably raises grader agreement over holistic scoring; holistic LLM judging tops out at human-level noise.
findings.evidence: TICK (arXiv 2410.03608, read via a digest because arxiv.org is blocked): generated checklists of YES/NO questions give "+5.8%" exact agreement with human preferences "compared to direct scoring"; giving the checklists to humans raised inter-annotator agreement "from 0.194 to 0.256". MT-Bench README: "humans and GPT-4 judge achieve over 80% agreement, the same level of agreement between humans." Anthropic develop-tests: "Automate when possible: Structure questions to allow for automated grading (for example, multiple-choice, string match, code-graded, LLM-graded)" and "Generally best practice to use a different model to evaluate than the model used to generate the evaluated output". (preprint via secondary mirror; vendor doc)
findings.implication: Write acceptance as atomic binary items (EARS or Given/When/Then), each with a runnable `check {cmd, expect_exit}`; the blind verdict is item-wise YES/NO on a different model from the implementer, never a 1-10 overall score.

findings.claim: Use constrained requirement syntax (EARS templates or declarative Given/When/Then that describes WHAT not HOW) for acceptance criteria; EARS maps 1:1 to test structure, but its published defect-reduction evidence could not be verified and Spec Kit does not standardize on it.
findings.evidence: EARS templates confirmed by multiple independent GitHub reproductions (primary alistairmavin.com blocked): `The <system> shall <response>`; `WHEN <trigger>, the <system> shall ...`; `WHILE <state>, ...`; `WHERE <feature>, ...`; `IF <unwanted condition>, THEN the <system> shall ...`. Kiro's requirements command (via cc-sdd replica; kiro.dev blocked) pairs each user story with EARS acceptance criteria. A practitioner ADR records that EARS->vitest mapping is a "deterministic 1:1 template-to-test transform" and that "GitHub Spec Kit does not standardize on EARS; it uses Given/When/Then scenarios with numbered FR-NNN requirements" (issue #1356 open). Cucumber docs source: "it should describe what, not how"; test "Will this wording need to change if the implementation does?"; prefer "When Free Frieda logs in with her valid credentials / Then she sees a Free article" over click-by-click steps. BMAD full-plan standard: "Testable: All acceptance criteria use Given/When/Then format", "Surface-anchored: ACs observe outermost surface, never internal proxies". (secondary mirror / vendor doc / practitioner)
findings.implication: Schema `acceptance[].form: ears|gwt|command` with a lint that rejects imperative UI steps and implementation terms; each AC must name an observable at the outermost surface so two graders and the test generator read it identically.

findings.claim: A literal one-block 'scope of consent' statement in the prompt reduced out-of-scope actions from 17.1% to 0.0% in a paired ablation, but agents match its text rather than infer boundaries, and model-layer defenses still miss about 17% of overeager actions, so the statement must be both stated and enforced.
findings.evidence: Qu et al. 2026, 'Overeager Coding Agents: Measuring Out-of-Scope Actions on Benign Tasks' (arXiv:2605.18583; read via an English digest and a full Chinese translation on GitHub because arxiv.org is blocked): overeager = reads/writes "the user never authorized" on a benign task; on prompt pairs byte-identical except the "Scope of consent" block, "stripping the consent declaration alone raises the overeager rate from 0.0% to 17.1% on paired scenarios (McNemar exact p = 2.4 x 10^-4)" (Claude Code, Sonnet-4.6); "Stripping consent multiplies the overeager rate on every shared base model (Delta in [11.9, 17.2] pp)"; permissive frameworks 5.4-27.7% vs ask-to-continue OpenHands 0.2-4.5%; 500 scenarios, ~7,500 runs; authors note agents were "matching declared text rather than inferring boundaries". Anthropic 'How we contain Claude': auto mode "catches roughly 83% of overeager behaviors before they execute", "~17% of overeager actions get through", "Design for containment at the environment layer first, then steer behavior at the model layer." (preprint via secondary mirror; vendor eng)
findings.implication: Every item carries `authorized_scope.statement` written literally ("May change: <paths>. Must not change: <paths/behaviours>. No irreversible actions.") plus `allow_paths`/`deny_paths`, and the intake compiles `deny_paths` into a PreToolUse deny hook for the implementer; the reviewer and verdict check that "nothing outside the task's scope changed".

findings.claim: Do not extract HOW (tech stack, APIs, code structure) at intake; file paths appear only as authorization boundaries, and the whole artifact must stay one page.
findings.evidence: Spec Kit spec-driven.md: "Focus on WHAT users need and WHY", "Avoid HOW to implement (no tech stack, APIs, code structure)", "Don't guess: If the prompt doesn't specify something, mark it"; specify checklist: "No implementation details (languages, frameworks, APIs)", "Success criteria are technology-agnostic". BMAD: a well-defined intent is "complete enough that someone else could build it without guessing, and no longer than that." Anthropic context engineering: "find the smallest possible set of high-signal tokens that maximize the likelihood of some desired outcome"; prompting golden rule: "Show your prompt to a colleague with minimal context on the task and ask them to follow it. If they'd be confused, Claude will be too." Tension: Claude Code says good specs "name the files and interfaces involved, state what is out of scope, and end with an end-to-end verification step" - resolved by putting files under scope, interfaces in the plan. (vendor doc / vendor eng)
findings.implication: A PostToolUse lint on `.funnel/intake/**` rejects framework/library/API names and code fences in `goal`/`acceptance[].text`, and a length gate keeps `intake.md` to one page; anything longer is design and moves to the plan stage.

findings.claim: The non-functional envelope has a fixed shape: BMAD's three build-gate statements (what should be true when done / what must not change / what is out of scope) plus intent gaps, irreversible actions and footprint; Spec Kit forces performance/constraints/scale to be stated or marked NEEDS CLARIFICATION.
findings.evidence: BMAD choose-a-planning-path: "Is the intent already well defined?" - it says "What should be true when the work is done", "What must not change", "What is out of scope". build-a-change: the plan reports "intent gaps (things you did not say that you would notice in the result)", "irreversible actions", and "footprint"; anything flagged needs "a full written plan first, with each intent gap recorded as an open question you answer before approval". Spec Kit plan template Technical Context: "Performance Goals: ... or NEEDS CLARIFICATION", "Constraints: e.g., <200ms p95, <100MB memory, offline-capable", "Scale/Scope: ... or NEEDS CLARIFICATION"; clarify categories include "Non-Functional Quality Attributes", "Integration & External Dependencies", "Edge Cases & Failure Handling", "Constraints & Tradeoffs". Claude Code /goal: "Constraints that matter: anything that must not change on the way there, such as 'no other test file is modified'". (practitioner framework / vendor doc)
findings.implication: Schema `nfr_envelope {performance, security, compatibility, out_of_scope[], footprint_cap}` and `authorized_scope.irreversible_actions_allowed` (default false), plus `risk_signals` for the router; an item routed to the funnel with any of the three statements blank is `needs-clarification`.

findings.claim: Ask at most five human questions, one at a time, each multiple-choice with a recommended default and ordered by impact times uncertainty; ask only when the answer would materially change implementation or validation, and never about standard practices or tech stack.
findings.evidence: Spec Kit /clarify: "Maximum of 5 total questions across the whole session"; "Present EXACTLY ONE question at a time"; "Never reveal future queued questions in advance"; options as a table with "**Recommended:**" and 1-2 sentences of reasoning; multiple-choice 2-5 mutually exclusive options or short answer <=5 words; prioritised by Impact x Uncertainty; gate "Would the answer materially change implementation or validation strategy?"; excludes implementation-only choices and tech-stack comparisons; stops when critical ambiguities are resolved, user says done, or 5 asked; else "No critical ambiguities detected worth formal clarification". /specify: "Maximum 3 [NEEDS CLARIFICATION] markers total", "Make informed guesses based on context and industry standards", "Use reasonable defaults for unspecified details (document assumptions in Assumptions section)", do not ask about data retention, performance targets, error handling, authentication methods, integration patterns. Claude Code AskUserQuestion is multiple-choice with an `Other` free-text row. (vendor doc)
findings.implication: Intake question budget: <=5 (<=3 when <=2 items), one at a time via AskUserQuestion with a recommended option; every question must pass the materiality gate and must not be answerable by code search or a spike; leftovers become `open_questions[]` with defaults.

findings.claim: Practitioners disagree on interview length: open-ended interviews (Claude Code, Harper Reed, Superpowers) vs generate-first-then-iterate (Kiro) vs ask-nothing-and-record-assumptions (BMAD headless); the reconciling rule is that questions happen before any workflow launches and unresolved high-impact gaps halt as blocked rather than being guessed.
findings.evidence: Claude Code: "Interview me in detail using the AskUserQuestion tool ... Keep interviewing until we've covered everything, then write a complete spec to SPEC.md", then "start a fresh session to execute it". Harper Reed: "Ask me one question at a time so we can develop a thorough, step-by-step spec for this idea" (but for legacy code "planning done per task, not for the entire project"). Superpowers: "Only one question per message". Kiro/cc-sdd: "Generate an initial set of requirements ... then iterate with the user to refine them" rather than sequential questioning. BMAD headless: "infer everything, ask nothing, but never invent - record inferences as `assumptions[]` and gaps that need a human as `open_questions[]`"; build-auto: "Do not fantasize or leave open questions. If the intent cannot be resolved, HALT with status `blocked`". Claude Code workflows: "No mid-run user input ... For sign-off between stages, run each stage as its own workflow"; scheduled tasks "can't ask clarifying questions". (vendor doc / practitioner)
findings.implication: Order is fixed: search -> assume with recorded defaults (owner, impact, revisit trigger) -> spike empirical unknowns -> ask <=5 -> halt `needs-clarification` on any remaining high-impact fork; the intake runs as its own stage before the Workflow script so the script never needs a human.

findings.claim: Prefer a time-boxed throwaway spike over a human question when the unknown is empirical (does it exist, what does the API return, is the test flaky), but spike last among splitting patterns, never first.
findings.evidence: Lawrence's patterns (via GitHub reproductions; humanizingwork.com blocked): "Spike (last resort) - Time-box investigation when team cannot estimate"; consensus digest of 20 story-splitting sources: "Spike last, not first." Claude Code: "tell Claude to try something risky. If it doesn't work, rewind and try a different approach"; "Vague prompts can be useful when you're exploring and can afford to course-correct."; agent teams: "Spawn 5 agent teammates to investigate different hypotheses. Have them talk to each other to try to disprove each other's theories". BMAD reviewer gate: "a throwaway prototype may run it quietly or skip the gate entirely". Spec Kit assess: ideas go through research ("evidence *against* the idea") and "go / needs-clarification / kill", and a `go` needs evidence "adequate or higher (never weak/unknown)". (practitioner / vendor doc; secondary for Lawrence)
findings.implication: Schema `spike {needed, question, timebox_minutes, throwaway: true, result}`; a spike's output is facts written into `assumptions`/`existing_code_check`, never code that survives; `idea`/`improve` asks may legitimately end in `kill`, recorded as a successful outcome.

findings.claim: Size every work item to one context window: one vertical slice with its tests and its check, walking skeleton first, split by workflow step / rule / path / interface / data / CRUD before resorting to a spike.
findings.evidence: Ralph README: "Each PRD item should be small enough to complete in one context window. If a task is too big, the LLM runs out of context before finishing and produces poor code."; prompt.md: "Work on ONE story per iteration", "Keep changes focused and minimal". Anthropic long-running harness: features like "a user can open a new chat, type in a query, press enter, and see an AI response", "work on only one feature at a time" was "critical to addressing the agent's tendency to do too much at once". Superpowers writing-plans: a task is "the smallest unit that carries its own test cycle". Agent teams: "self-contained units that produce a clear deliverable, such as a function, a test file, or a review". Spec Kit: "Each user story/journey must be INDEPENDENTLY TESTABLE". Cockburn (quoted verbatim in two repos): a walking skeleton is "a tiny implementation of the system that performs a small end-to-end function ... it should link together the main architectural components." Lawrence's nine patterns and SPIDR (Spikes, Paths, Interfaces, Data, Rules) reproduced consistently in several skill repos (primary sites blocked). (practitioner / vendor eng / secondary)
findings.implication: Schema `size {files_est, fits_one_context, walking_skeleton}`; the splitter re-runs until every item passes a size check (roughly <=10 files, one commit, one check) and the distributor gives each item to one subagent with `maxTurns` and a summary return.

findings.claim: Definition of done should be an ordered list of commands with expected exit codes, evaluated by a separate model or a deterministic hook rather than by the agent that did the work.
findings.evidence: Claude Code best practices: "Give Claude something that produces a pass or fail, and the loop closes on its own"; "Claude stops when the work looks done. Without a check it can run, 'looks done' is the only signal available"; /goal: a good condition has "One measurable end state", "A stated check: how Claude should prove it, such as `npm test` exits 0 or `git status` is clean", and the evaluator is "a fresh model rather than the one doing the work". Hooks: Stop exit 2 "Prevents Claude from stopping"; "Claude Code overrides a Stop hook after it blocks eight times in a row without progress" (check `stop_hook_active`); prompt-based hooks return `ok:false` with a `reason` or `impossible:true`. Ralph: `passes: true` only after typecheck/lint/test. Superpowers: "NO COMPLETION CLAIMS WITHOUT FRESH VERIFICATION EVIDENCE". (vendor doc / practitioner)
findings.implication: Every `acceptance[].check` is `{cmd, expect_exit, expect_output_regex}`; the intake emits a `done.sh` the implementer's Stop hook and the reviewers run verbatim, so pass/fail is identical for the implementer, the independent reviewer and the blind verdict.

findings.claim: The context-free verdict agent must receive only a contract subset of the intake (restated goal, acceptance text and checks, scope statement, out-of-scope) delivered as a fresh subagent task message; reviewers must be told to report gaps against the stated requirements only.
findings.evidence: Claude Code sub-agents: "Each subagent starts with a fresh, isolated context window. It doesn't see your conversation history, the skills you've already invoked, or the files Claude has already read." Best practices adversarial review: "A reviewer running in a fresh subagent context sees only the diff and the criteria you give it, not the reasoning that produced the change"; prompt: "Check that every requirement is implemented, the listed edge cases have tests, and nothing outside the task's scope changed. Report gaps, not style preferences."; caveat: "A reviewer prompted to find gaps will usually report some, even when the work is sound". Superpowers subagent-driven development: reviewers get "task brief, report file, diff as a file, binding global constraints" and "A dispatch prompt describes one task, not the session's history." Anthropic multi-agent: each brief needs "an objective, an output format, guidance on the tools and sources to use, and clear task boundaries". (vendor doc / practitioner)
findings.implication: Schema field `verdict_view` lists the exact paths the verdict agent may see (excluding verbatim ask, assumptions, open questions, risk signals); the verdict prompt is item-wise YES/NO plus a scope check, and the in-process independent reviewers get the full artifact.

findings.claim: Requirement-quality checks can themselves be written as binary checklist items ('unit tests for requirements'), giving a deterministic intake lint for vagueness, gaps and conflicts.
findings.evidence: Spec Kit checklist command: "checklists are unit tests for requirements writing"; items must be interrogative and test the requirement, e.g. "Are featured episode counts and layouts explicitly specified?", "Can visual hierarchy be objectively measured?" rather than "Verify landing page displays 3 cards"; format `- [ ] CHK### - Are [requirement aspect] defined/specified for [scenario]? [Quality Dimension, Spec section or Gap]` with `[Gap]/[Ambiguity]/[Conflict]` markers. Spec Kit specify: "Every vague requirement should fail the 'testable and unambiguous' checklist item". Anthropic define-success: criteria must be Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant; "Even 'hazy' topics such as ethics and safety can be quantified." (vendor doc)
findings.implication: The intake release gate runs a fixed checklist (vague adjectives quantified? every AC has a check? scope statement literal? out-of-scope listed? bug has repro?) as a prompt-based hook with a small model; failures return the artifact to intake instead of leaking ambiguity downstream.

findings.claim: Every intake rule should have a deterministic home in Claude Code: UserPromptSubmit to stamp or refuse prompts, Workflow output schemas to validate the artifact, PreToolUse to enforce deny paths, TaskCreated to block duplicate or compound tasks, Stop/prompt hooks to gate completion.
findings.evidence: Hooks reference: UserPromptSubmit exit 2 "Blocks prompt processing and erases the prompt", stdout/`hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext` adds context, `updatedInput` modifies the prompt; PreToolUse exit 2 "Blocks the tool call"; Stop exit 2 "Prevents Claude from stopping" with an 8-block cap. Agent teams: TaskCreated "Exit with code 2 to prevent creation and send feedback", TaskCompleted likewise. Workflows: `agent()` with `schema` returns validated JSON, "If the subagent's output still fails validation after five attempts, the call fails"; `omitClaudeMd` and `isolation: worktree` on subagents. Best practices: "Unlike CLAUDE.md instructions which are advisory, hooks are deterministic and guarantee the action happens." (vendor doc)
findings.implication: Implement the intake as a Workflow stage whose agents return `intake.json` under a schema, plus three hooks (PostToolUse lint on `.funnel/intake/**`, PreToolUse deny-path guard compiled from the artifact, TaskCreated duplicate/compound guard); advisory prose in CLAUDE.md is kept to the few rules that cannot be scripted.

anti_patterns: Relying on the one-sentence scope statement alone for safety: the Overeager paper shows agents match its text rather than infer boundaries, and Anthropic reports model-layer defenses still let ~17% of overeager actions through; the statement must also be compiled into PreToolUse deny rules / sandbox paths.

Grading acceptance holistically on a 1-10 scale: MT-Bench judges top out at 'over 80% agreement, the same level of agreement between humans', and a reviewer 'prompted to find gaps will usually report some, even when the work is sound'; decomposed binary checklist items are what raise agreement (TICK +5.8%).

Unbounded interviews for brownfield work: Harper Reed himself switches to 'planning done per task' on legacy code, Spec Kit caps at 5 questions / 3 markers, Kiro generates-then-iterates; and Claude Code workflows allow 'No mid-run user input', so questions asked inside an orchestrated run stall it.

Asking the human what the codebase can answer: every Ralph/Superpowers/Spec Kit source says search first ('Never guess at file paths', 'Search the codebase before assuming functionality is missing'); such questions burn the budget and anchor the human on the agent's misunderstanding.

Extracting HOW at intake (tech stack, APIs, class names, imperative UI steps): Spec Kit 'Avoid HOW', Cucumber 'Will this wording need to change if the implementation does?'; it removes design freedom and makes acceptance criteria brittle and grader-dependent.

Large items to save orchestration overhead: Ralph ('runs out of context before finishing and produces poor code'), Anthropic's harness ('tendency to do too much at once') and agent-teams docs ('teammates work too long without check-ins') all report degradation past one feature per context window.

Deciding scope at task-selection or implementation time instead of at intake/plan time (ralph-orchestrator anti-pattern 'Scoping work at task selection time'): the implementer then expands scope inside its own context, which is exactly where overeager edits originate.

Fixing a bug before reproducing it: Superpowers 'NO FIXES WITHOUT ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION FIRST'; Spec Kit reports an unperformed reproduction as partial/not-run, and the RED run is what lets a later blind verdict prove the fix.

Treating 'kill' or 'needs-clarification' as failure: Spec Kit's assess pipeline records kill 'as successful, not a failure' and BMAD halts as `blocked` rather than guessing; forcing every ask through to implementation is how ambiguity reaches the last stage.

Encoding intake rules as long advisory prose (a bloated CLAUDE.md): Claude Code warns 'If your CLAUDE.md is too long, Claude ignores half of it'; mechanical rules belong in hooks and schema validation, not instructions.
open_questions: No accessible controlled study compares EARS vs Gherkin vs free text for LLM-grader agreement on code acceptance criteria; the TICK numbers are for general instruction checklists. A small in-house experiment (same 20 ACs in three formats, two fresh Haiku graders, exact agreement) would settle which form the intake should mandate.

The 0.0% -> 17.1% scope-statement result is a paired ablation on one model/framework and the authors say agents text-match the block; does a literal path-level statement still work when the implementer is a subagent that never saw the human's prompt, and across models?

What question budget suits a solo vibe-coder: Spec Kit uses 5 questions / 3 markers, interviews are unbounded, BMAD headless asks none; the proposed 3-for-small / 5-otherwise split is an inference, not measured.

Should the context-free verdict agent see the scope statement and out-of-scope list (needed to judge scope creep) or does that anchor it on the intake's framing? Proposed: contract yes (goal, ACs, scope), process no (assumptions, questions, risk signals).

Hamel Husain's binary-vs-Likert judge argument and Mavin's EARS outcome data (RE'09, Rolls-Royce) are widely cited but were unreachable through the proxy (hamel.dev, alistairmavin.com, IEEE, arXiv blocked); they remain unverified here.

Spec Kit's extension command files are named `speckit.assess.intake.md` / `speckit.bug.assess.md` under `extensions/*/commands/`, while the README slugs are `/speckit-assess-intake`; the installed version should be checked before scripting against either.
How to handle language drift: the intake keeps the ask verbatim (Russian) and restates in English; whether a back-translation check catches lost nuance cheaply enough is untested.

value.dimension: The funnel as a state machine: on-disk ledger, send-back semantics, bounded loops, adjudication, and human approval points designed for a non-reading approver

findings.claim: Claude Code's Stop/SubagentStop hooks are overridden after 8 consecutive continuations (CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_BLOCK_CAP, 0 disables) and a hook must exit early when stop_hook_active is true; the docs disagree on whether the cap counts all blocks or only blocks 'without progress'.
findings.evidence: hooks doc: 'Claude Code applies an 8-consecutive-continuation cap: after stop hooks have continued the turn eight times in a row, Claude Code overrides the next block and ends the turn.' env-vars: 'Maximum number of consecutive times a Stop or SubagentStop hook may block ... (default: 8). Set to 0 to disable the cap.' hooks-guide: 'overrides a Stop hook after it blocks eight times in a row without progress.'
findings.implication: Treat the 8-cap as a substrate backstop only. The funnel's loop governor is a counter in the on-disk ledger; the Stop hook reads state.json and allows the stop as soon as the ledger says 'escalate', so the cap never decides. Add a verification test for the 'without progress' wording.

findings.claim: /goal is a transcript-only Haiku judge: it never runs tools, judges only what Claude surfaced, stops after several turns with no tool use, and needs a turn cap written into the condition.
findings.evidence: 'The evaluator judges your condition against what Claude has surfaced in the conversation. It doesn't run commands or read files independently'; 'It does not call tools, so it can only judge what Claude has already surfaced'; 'If Claude keeps answering the evaluator without making progress (no tool use for several turns in a row), Claude Code stops the loop'; 'include a turn or time clause in the condition, such as or stop after 20 turns'.
findings.implication: Never use /goal (or any prompt-based Stop hook) as the authoritative verifier; it is exactly the judge a printed 'all tests pass' line can fool. Authoritative gates must re-execute checks: command Stop hooks, TaskCompleted hooks, or a CI runner writing evidence/<sha>/tests.json.

findings.claim: Dynamic workflows cannot take mid-run user input, have no filesystem, replay deterministically, and a failed agent reruns every agent started after it; resume works only in the same session or a --resume of it, and a fresh session gets 'nothing to resume'.
findings.evidence: Constraints table: 'No mid-run user input ... For sign-off between stages, run each stage as its own workflow'; 'No direct filesystem or shell access from the workflow itself'; resume: 'Failed: runs again, and so does every agent that started after it, even ones that completed'; 'If a script starts A, B, C, and D in that order and B fails, relaunching returns A from cache and runs B, C, and D again'; 'In a session you start fresh, Claude has no earlier run to relaunch'; 'Date.now(), Math.random() ... throw'; 5 schema attempts (MAX_STRUCTURED_OUTPUT_RETRIES); 16 concurrent agents; 1,000 agents per run.
findings.implication: One workflow per stage between human gates. Every agent must persist its result into .workflow/<id>/ before returning so a fresh session restarts from ledger state, not replay. Order agent() calls cheap/deterministic first and flaky last to shrink rerun blast radius; pass run_id/timestamp via args.

findings.claim: Subagents start with fresh context; omitClaudeMd (v2.1.271+) removes CLAUDE.md; isolation: worktree branches from the repository's DEFAULT branch, not the parent's HEAD, unless worktree.baseRef is 'head'; maxTurns returns output marked partial (v2.1.246+) that can be resumed via SendMessage.
findings.evidence: 'Each subagent starts with a fresh, isolated context window'; 'giving it an isolated copy of the repository branched by default from your default branch rather than the parent session's HEAD'; worktrees doc: 'Subagent worktrees use the same base branch as --worktree, so they branch from your repository's default branch unless worktree.baseRef is set to "head"'; 'Claude Code returns its output marked as partial, and Claude can resume it'.
findings.implication: A worktree-isolated reviewer on defaults would review main, not the item branch: set worktree.baseRef:'head' or hand it the sha explicitly. The context-free L2 verdict agent = omitClaudeMd:true + tools allowlist + a delegation prompt containing only the frozen spec, the sha and neutral evidence.

findings.claim: permissions.deny rules block in every mode including bypassPermissions, PreToolUse hooks run before the prompt and an exit-2 hook precedes allow rules, but hook 'allow' can never override deny rules; whether a hook DENY holds under --dangerously-skip-permissions is not documented.
findings.evidence: permission-modes: 'Deny rules block in every mode, including bypassPermissions ... Allow rules have no effect in bypassPermissions'; permissions: 'Hook decisions don't bypass permission rules. Claude Code evaluates deny and ask rules regardless of what a PreToolUse hook returns'; 'A hook that exits with code 2 stops the tool call before permission rules are evaluated'; auto mode: 'if the classifier blocks an action 3 times in a row or 20 times total, auto mode pauses'.
findings.implication: Encode irreversible-action guards (migrations, force push, deletes, deploys, payments) as permissions.deny rules, which are documented to survive bypass mode; use hooks for ledger-state checks (e.g., no commit unless state==IMPLEMENT). Put 'hook deny under bypass' on the verification checklist.

findings.claim: Claude Code checkpoints and ~/.claude state are unsuitable as the durable ledger: checkpoints ignore Bash and subagent edits, keep 100 snapshots for ~30 days, and the shared task list under ~/.claude/tasks is swept after cleanupPeriodDays (default 30 days).
findings.evidence: checkpointing: 'Checkpointing does not track files modified by Bash commands'; 'Any other subagent: rewinding doesn't restore the edits. Use git to revert them'; 'file snapshots for the 100 most recent checkpoints'; 'about 30 days'; agent-teams: 'Task list: ~/.claude/tasks/{team-name}/ ... Retention is governed by the same cleanupPeriodDays'; claude-directory: 'The default is 30 days'.
findings.implication: The ledger must live in the repository on the item branch (.workflow/<id>/, committed with checkpoint commits and tags). 'Reset' on a recycle is a git reset to the last passing checkpoint tag, never /rewind.

findings.claim: Anthropic's long-running harness makes the feature list immutable except for a passes flag, forbids editing/removing tests, bootstraps each fresh session from a progress file plus git log, works one feature at a time, and found premature 'done' marking to be the main failure until end-to-end self-verification was required.
findings.evidence: 'We prompt coding agents to edit this file only by changing the status of a passes field ... It is unacceptable to remove or edit tests'; 'a way for agents to quickly understand the state of work when starting with a fresh context window ... the claude-progress.txt file alongside the git history'; 'work on only one feature at a time'; 'Claude marked features as done prematurely' -> 'Only mark features as passing after careful testing' with browser automation.
findings.implication: acceptance.json is the funnel's feature_list.json: criteria and their test set are frozen with the spec (hash recorded); the implementer may not edit tests or criteria (deny rule on those paths); the passes flag is flipped by the neutral verifier, not the author.

findings.claim: Fresh context beats continued context after a wrong turn: LLMs lose ~39% in multi-turn vs single-turn settings, mostly as unreliability, and 'when LLMs take a wrong turn in a conversation, they get lost and do not recover'; Claude Code's guidance is to /clear after two failed corrections and to execute specs and reviews in fresh sessions.
findings.evidence: Laban et al. abstract: 'an average drop of 39% across six generation tasks'; 'a minor loss in aptitude and a significant increase in unreliability'; 'LLMs often make assumptions in early turns and prematurely attempt to generate final solutions, on which they overly rely'. Best practices: 'After two failed corrections, /clear and write a better initial prompt incorporating what you learned'; 'A fresh context improves code review since Claude won't be biased toward code it just wrote'.
findings.implication: A recycle that lands on a fresh implementer carries the rewritten spec, learned constraints and reproducible failures as failing tests, and never the conversation or the failing WIP diff. Committed, test-passing checkpoints in git history are allowed; the discarded diff is not attached as a hint (no source shows a benefit, and over-reliance on early attempts is the documented failure).

findings.claim: superpowers' explicit ladder: review rounds 1-3 resume the same implementer with findings verbatim; rounds 4-5 dispatch a fresh implementer on a more capable model; hard cap 5 rounds then the human adjudicates each open finding; every fix ends with a scoped re-review of only the fix diff; the reviewer gets diff+plan and never the session history; three failed fixes means stop and question the architecture.
findings.evidence: subagent-driven-development: 'Rounds 1-3: resume the original implementer'; 'Rounds 4-5: dispatch a fresh implementer on a more capable model'; 'adjudicate each open finding yourself' after round 5; 'scoped re-review verifying only the fix diff'. requesting-code-review: reviewer receives 'precisely crafted context only — never your session history'. systematic-debugging: 'If ≥ 3: STOP and question the architecture'. verification-before-completion: 'NO COMPLETION CLAIMS WITHOUT FRESH VERIFICATION EVIDENCE'.
findings.implication: Adopt as the default review ladder (same implementer ->stronger fresh -> re-decompose -> human), with counts 3/5 justified by cross-source convergence (Claude Code's 'two failed corrections', superpowers' 3 strikes and 5 rounds), but make stalls, not rounds, consume rungs.
