findings.claim: OpenHands' StuckDetector gives mechanical stall thresholds: 4 identical action-observation pairs, 3 identical actions each yielding an error, 3 repeated agent messages without observations, or an A-O-A'-O' alternation over the last 6 steps, with equality normalized to ignore PIDs and thought text.
findings.evidence: stuck.py (v0.20.0): _is_stuck_repeating_action_observation checks 'a loop of 4 identical action-observation pairs'; repeated action/error at 3; monologue at 3 MessageActions with source=AGENT; alternating pattern over six recent steps; _eq_no_pid ignores command_id and compares command and exit_code; in interactive mode only events after the last user message are examined.
findings.implication: Define progress_hash = sha256(sorted failing-test ids) + sha256(normalized verify command + exit code) + diff distance of the fix. Two consecutive identical hashes, or an A/B/A/B alternation over 4 rounds, is a stall; two stalls escalate a rung regardless of the round count, so the cap counts stalls, not iterations.

findings.claim: RLHF models are sycophantic and humans and preference models prefer convincingly-written sycophantic answers a non-negligible fraction of the time; the 'are you sure' eval shows models capitulating when merely challenged; self-preference (evaluators favor their own generations) and U-Sophistry (models learn to convince evaluators when wrong, including code that passes human unit tests) were reported but their primary sources were blocked here.
findings.evidence: Anthropic: 'both humans and preference models (PMs) prefer convincingly-written sycophantic responses over correct ones a non-negligible fraction of the time'; 'sycophancy is a general behavior of RLHF models'. sycophancy-eval README: are_you_sure set — model 'apologizes and provides a corrected answer without independent verification'. Panickssery et al. (arXiv 2404.13076) and Wen et al. (arXiv 2409.12822) blocked; claims from memory of abstracts.
findings.implication: The author never argues in-context: a fresh 'defender' agent that sees only code+finding+tests writes any rebuttal as commands and outputs; the L2 verdict uses a different session and preferably a different model family; the adjudicator re-executes every cited command in a clean worktree and never accepts pasted output.

findings.claim: Debate between two persuasive agents judged by a third improves judge accuracy over a single-advocate 'consultancy' protocol, so contested findings should be settled by symmetric debate, not by one side explaining itself.
findings.evidence: ucl-dark/llm_debate README: protocols 'blind, consultancy, debate, interactive debate, expert judge' on QuALITY; 'when debaters are optimized for persuasiveness rather than accuracy, judges achieve higher correctness rates compared to consultancy and baseline approaches'. The paper's exact accuracies (debate ~76% LLM / ~88% human judges vs ~48%/60% naive) are from memory because arXiv/PMLR were blocked.
findings.implication: Only CONTESTED findings (both sides hold reproducible evidence) go to a two-agent debate with randomly assigned sides, 2 rounds, judged by a fresh adjudicator with an explicit 'Unknown' option; Unknown escalates to the human. Never a single-advocate format.

findings.claim: Reward hacking is observed in coding environments (fake test passes via sys.exit(0); 12% sabotage of detection), so graders must be hack-resistant and grade final environment state, with LLM rubrics calibrated against humans and given an 'Unknown' exit.
findings.evidence: 'calling sys.exit(0) in Python to break out of a test harness with an exit code of 0, making it appear that all tests have passed successfully'; '12% of the time, the model would intentionally attempt to sabotage the code in ways that would reduce our ability to detect reward hacking'. Evals guide: 'Make your graders resistant to bypasses or hacks'; 'The outcome is the final state in the environment'; 'give the LLM a way out, like providing an instruction to return Unknown'.
findings.implication: Verification evidence is produced only by a neutral runner (hook/CI) that parses test counts and exit codes, checks test-file hashes against the frozen spec, and writes evidence/<sha>/; transcript judges are advisory. The 'Haiku judge fooled by all-tests-pass text' test belongs on the verification checklist.

findings.claim: Approvals must bind to a commit: GitHub branch protection can dismiss stale approvals when new commits change the diff, require the most recent reviewable push to be approved by someone other than the pusher, require status checks and conversation resolution; Claude Code's hosted Code Review check is always neutral and never blocks, exposing a machine-readable severity line instead.
findings.evidence: github/docs: 'dismiss stale pull request approvals when commits are pushed that affect the diff'; 'the most recent reviewable push must be approved by someone other than the person who pushed it'; 'Required status checks must have a successful, skipped, or neutral status'. code-review doc: 'The check run always completes with a neutral conclusion so it never blocks merging ... read the severity breakdown from the check run output in your own CI' (bughunter-severity JSON).
findings.implication: approvals.json and verdict.json are keyed by sha; any new head sha sets valid:false on all of them; an approval recorded by the implementer's own session id is rejected; landing requires L2 sha == human-approval sha == branch head and an up-to-date base. Write your own required check that reads approvals.json.

findings.claim: Claude Code's own reviewer design uses many narrow finders plus a verification step that filters false positives, a citation bar for findings, nit caps, and an explicit re-review convergence rule, because unbounded nit loops reach 'round seven on style alone'.
findings.evidence: 'Each agent looks for a different class of issue, then a verification step checks candidates against actual code behavior to filter out false positives'; REVIEW.md guidance: 'behavior claims need a file:line citation in the source, not an inference from naming'; 'after the first review, suppress new nits and post Important findings only stops a one-line fix from reaching round seven on style alone'; best practices: 'A reviewer prompted to find gaps will usually report some, even when the work is sound'.
findings.implication: Finding schema: a Critical/Important finding must carry file:line and a reproduction or failing test, otherwise it cannot block; after round 1 only Critical/Important may reopen the loop; minors are batched and never recycle; a finding refuted by adjudication is blacklisted for re-raise by the same tier, which prevents reviewer-tier ping-pong.

findings.claim: For a non-reading approver, the evidence pack (test output, commands and results, screenshots) beats re-running or reading, review must be risk-tiered with a risk-weighted human sample, and the observed failure mode of frequent approvals is rubber-stamping.
findings.evidence: best practices: 'Have Claude show evidence rather than asserting success: the test output, the command it ran and what it returned, or a screenshot of the result. Reviewing evidence is faster than re-running the verification yourself'; 'After the tenth approval you're clicking through rather than reviewing'. Anthropic SDLC: 'We tier our codebase by risk ... A risk-weighted sample is reviewed by humans ... invariants like user A can never read user B's data ... triggers additional manual reviews'; 'reserving human review for regulated or truly critical code'.
findings.implication: Human gate = one generated screen: acceptance checklist with pass/fail and evidence links, screenshots/recorded run, risk summary, verdict sentences, cost, open unverifiable items, and Go/Recycle(stage)/Hold/Kill. Tier 0 auto-lands under sampling (start 10-20%), tier 1 batched digest, tier 2 blocking; cap decisions per sitting and order by risk then age.

findings.claim: AI adoption raises throughput but still reduces delivery stability unless automated testing, mature version control and fast feedback loops exist; Google's review practice sets one business day as the maximum response time and ~100 lines as a reasonable change size.
findings.evidence: DORA 2025 via Google Cloud: 'AI adoption does continue to have a negative relationship with software delivery stability ... Without robust control systems, like strong automated testing, mature version control practices, and fast feedback loops, an increase in change volume leads to instability'. eng-practices: 'One business day is the maximum time it should take to respond'; 'most complaints about the code review process are actually resolved by making the process faster'; small CLs: 'Reviewed more quickly ... Less likely to introduce bugs ... Simpler to roll back'; '100 lines is usually a reasonable size'.
findings.implication: Decomposition targets slices of roughly 100-300 changed lines with their own acceptance criteria; the human gate has a one-business-day SLA after which tier-0 auto-lands under sampling and tier-1 re-pings; 'LGTM with comments' means minors never block landing.

findings.claim: Human input surfaces in Claude Code are narrow: AskUserQuestion works only where a person can answer (auto-continue via askUserQuestionTimeout), is denied in dontAsk and removed by --permission-prompts none, workflows have no mid-run input, agent teams auto-approve teammate plans, and TaskCompleted exit 2 blocks a task from being marked done.
findings.evidence: tools-reference: 'Questions stay open until you answer them'; askUserQuestionTimeout '60s, 5m, or 10m'. headless: 'AskUserQuestion ... are denied even when an allow rule matches' (dontAsk); '--permission-prompts none ... removes the tools that need an answer from a person, such as AskUserQuestion'. agent-teams: 'Claude Code approves the plan in the lead's session as soon as the request arrives, without the lead reviewing it'. hooks: TaskCompleted 'Exit code 2: the task is not marked as completed'.
findings.implication: Interactive gate: the stage workflow ends, then the main session asks via AskUserQuestion with a timeout that defers rather than blocks. Unattended gate: ledger state HUMAN_GATE mirrored as a GitHub required check. Agent teams cannot host a human gate. TaskCompleted hooks enforce 'no done without evidence/<sha>/tests.json'.

findings.claim: Existing spec/plan tools converge on per-item folders plus an archive step and an append-only learnings file: Spec Kit (spec/plan/tasks + constitution as gates, analyze/checklist), OpenSpec (changes/<name>/{proposal,design,tasks,specs}, archive merges deltas into living specs), GSD Core (.planning STATE.md/CONTEXT.md, fresh 200k-token executors, verify phase), Ralph (prd.json passes flag, append-only progress.txt, AGENTS.md learnings, max_iterations default 10).
findings.evidence: OpenSpec README: Propose -> Apply -> Archive, 'Move completed changes to archive/ and merge their specs into main specs'. GSD Core: 'solves context rot ... heavy work runs in fresh subagents' each with 'a clean 200k-token context'; STATE.md and CONTEXT.md 'survive session boundaries'. Ralph: 'Each iteration is a fresh instance with clean context'; 'progress.txt maintains an append-only log'; './scripts/ralph/ralph.sh [max_iterations]' default 10; completion '<promise>COMPLETE</promise>' when all passes:true. Spec Kit: constitution articles 'act as gates within the implementation planning process'.
findings.implication: Ledger layout .workflow/<id>/{state.json, intake.md, triage.json, plan.md, hypotheses.json, spec.vN.md, acceptance.json, constraints.md, progress.md, evidence/<sha>/, review-N.json, adjudication-*.json, verdict.json, approvals.json, cost.json} with archive/<id>/ on DONE and spec deltas merged into living docs; state.json is the single machine-readable truth, markdown is for humans.

findings.claim: Evidence that human decision quality decays with decision count (Danziger et al. 2011 parole study) is contested in magnitude (Weinshall-Margel & Shapard 2011 letter on non-random case ordering) and its primary sources were unreachable here, as was Parasuraman & Manzey 2010 on automation complacency.
findings.evidence: PNAS DOIs 10.1073/pnas.1018033108 and 10.1073/pnas.1110910108 and the Human Factors article were blocked by the egress proxy; the summary (favorable rulings ~65% after breaks falling toward zero; rebuttal that unrepresented prisoners were scheduled last) is from memory and not re-verified.
findings.implication: Do not build gate policy on a specific fatigue number. Use the directly observed engineering effect instead (Claude Code docs: 'After the tenth approval you're clicking through') and design for it: few decisions per sitting, defaults, batching, and sampling.

anti_patterns: Counting iterations instead of stalls: the five inconsistent caps (2 corrections, 3 strikes, 5 rounds, 8 Stop-hook blocks, 10 Ralph iterations) each count different things; a raw count wastes budget on obviously stuck loops and kills converging ones. OpenHands escalates on identical repeats (3-4) and A/B alternation, not counts.

Attaching the failing WIP diff to a send-back: Laban et al. show models over-rely on early attempts and do not recover; Claude Code best practices say the polluting element is 'failed approaches'. Only committed, test-passing checkpoints in git may travel.

Letting the author answer the reviewer inside its own context: sycophancy ('are you sure' capitulation), self-preference and learned persuasion make the outcome depend on rhetoric; rebuttals must be evidence produced by a fresh defender and re-executed by an adjudicator.
Using /goal, a prompt Stop hook, or a Haiku transcript grader as the gate: it 'does not call tools' and only sees what Claude surfaced; sys.exit(0)-style hacks make transcripts lie.

Relying on Claude Code checkpoints or ~/.claude/tasks as the ledger: Bash and subagent edits are not tracked, both are swept after ~30 days, and a fresh session cannot replay a workflow ('nothing to resume').

Placing the human gate inside a workflow or an agent team: workflows have 'No mid-run user input', teams auto-approve teammate plans, and dontAsk / --permission-prompts none deny or remove AskUserQuestion.
Reviewing from a default isolation: worktree subagent: it branches from the default branch, so it reviews main instead of the item branch unless worktree.baseRef is 'head' or the sha is handed over.

Guarding irreversible actions with hooks or prompts alone: only permissions.deny rules are documented to hold in bypassPermissions; hook 'allow' cannot override deny, and hook-deny under bypass is undocumented.

Unbounded nit loops between reviewer tiers: Claude Code's REVIEW.md guidance exists because 'a one-line fix' can reach 'round seven on style alone'; minors must never recycle and refuted findings must be blacklisted from re-raise.
Approving once and letting commits pile up: GitHub dismisses stale approvals for a reason; an approval without a sha binding approves nothing.

Big slices: Google treats ~1000 lines as too large; DORA 2025 finds more change volume without testing/version-control controls yields instability; large items also make the human evidence pack unreadable.
Trusting 'tools: Read, Grep, Bash' as read-only for a reviewer: Bash can write files and mutate git; use disallowedTools, a PreToolUse write guard, and worktree isolation.
Fanning out before the fragile step in a workflow: a failed agent reruns every agent started after it, so an early fan-out followed by a flaky agent re-bills the whole fan-out on relaunch.

Many human approvals per sitting: the documented outcome is rubber-stamping ('After the tenth approval you're clicking through rather than reviewing'), regardless of the contested decision-fatigue literature.
open_questions: Does the Stop-hook 8-cap count every consecutive block or only blocks 'without progress' (hooks-guide wording), and how is 'progress' defined internally? Needs a controlled test on the installed version.
Does an exit-2 PreToolUse hook still fire and block under --dangerously-skip-permissions? Deny rules are documented to hold; hooks are not.
For claude -p with --json-schema, are the 5 validation attempts per turn or per run, and do failed attempts consume --max-turns?
Can the /goal Haiku evaluator be fooled by a printed 'All tests passed' line with no tool use? The docs strongly imply yes; confirm before any reliance.
Should .workflow/ be committed to main at landing (auditable, OpenSpec-style archive) or kept only on item branches to avoid noise? No source addresses ledger noise on main.
What sampling rate for auto-landed tier-0 items is adequate? Anthropic reports a 'risk-weighted sample' without a number; Meta/Google risk-scoring sources were blocked.
Is a different model family for the L2 verdict necessary, or does a fresh session with omitClaudeMd already break self-preference? Panickssery et al. could not be read here.
Cooper's original gate literature (must-meet vs should-meet criteria, gatekeepers, 'gates with teeth') was unreachable; the Go/Recycle/Hold/Kill mapping follows the prior sweep's summary.
BMAD's '5 repair iterations, one ticket per autonomous run' could not be re-verified (docs/user-guide.md 404, README is marketing-only).

How much of the evidence pack can be generated deterministically (test counts, hashes, screenshots) versus written by an agent (risk narrative, 'what could go wrong'), and should the narrative author be the L2 reviewer or a fourth agent?

value.dimension: The context-free verdict: black-box acceptance across project types, minimal packet, anti-manipulation, and universal check adapters

findings.claim: 'No context' must mean no PROCESS context (plan, transcript, reviews, commit/PR prose, provenance), not no reference: every verified recipe gives the outside reviewer criteria/contract and, in the strongest ones, a running artifact; an ask-only reviewer has no oracle and invents gaps.
findings.evidence: Best practices: a fresh-context reviewer 'sees only the diff and the criteria you give it, not the reasoning that produced the change' and 'A reviewer prompted to find gaps will usually report some, even when the work is sound'. Harness post: the evaluator receives the sprint contract ('what done looked like... before any code was written') and uses Playwright 'the way a user would'. /goal docs: the tool-less evaluator 'doesn't run commands or read files independently'. FastChat judge_prompts.jsonl: MT-Bench's math judge is explicitly reference-guided ('Begin your evaluation by comparing the assistant's answer with the reference answer').
findings.implication: Design the outside tier as two de-correlated sub-tiers with a minimal hash-bound packet: Tier B (behavioral: ask + behavior-phrased criteria + runner recipe + artifact@SHA + artifact@merge-base; never sees code/diff/prose) and Tier C (code-reading: ask + criteria + comment-stripped diff + base tree; never sees transcript/plan/reviews/PR prose). A script, not a model, computes the verdict from both.

findings.claim: The four candidate packets have disjoint judging power: only the runnable-artifact packet can judge behavior and (with a baseline) regressions; only the diff packet can judge scope creep and code-level security; neither alone judges regressions without a merge-base baseline.
findings.evidence: Harness post: evaluator exercised 'UI features, API endpoints, and database states' in the running app; ultrareview: 'every reported finding is independently reproduced and verified'; best-practices review prompt checks 'nothing outside the task's scope changed' from the diff; Playwright/DVC/Terraform all judge by diffing candidate vs stored baseline ('On first execution, Playwright test will generate reference screenshots. Subsequent runs will compare against the reference'; 'dvc metrics diff' reports 'numeric difference (delta) from the previous value').
findings.implication: Always build and capture the merge-base artifact alongside the candidate so Tier B judges regressions as a diff of observations; reserve scope-creep and secret/auth findings for Tier C; treat 'ask + criteria' alone as a checklist, never a verdict.

findings.claim: The diff and its surrounding prose are an attacker-controlled channel: Anthropic's own action security doc names hidden HTML comments, invisible characters and hidden attributes as injection vectors, and a trained model will fake test success and even sabotage detection code.
findings.evidence: claude-code-action security.md: 'External contributors may include hidden instructions through HTML comments, invisible characters, hidden attributes, or other techniques' and sanitization 'new bypass techniques may emerge'. Reward-hacking research: models learned 'calling sys.exit(0) in Python to break out of a test harness with an exit code of 0' and '12% of the time, the model would intentionally attempt to sabotage the code in ways that would reduce our ability to detect reward hacking'. Null-model repo: a constant response reaches win_rate 76.9 / length-controlled 86.46 on AlpacaEval 2.0. CALM dataset README: refinement-aware bias = 'whether the LLM judge produces a different result when it is informed about the refinement'; bandwagon prompt injects 'number=90' percent agreement.
findings.implication: Tier B receives zero implementer text; Tier C receives the diff with comments/docstrings stripped, from a history-less archive (no git log/commit messages, no gh/PR body), with a hidden-Unicode/HTML-comment scan that converts injection attempts into findings; the runner counts executed tests rather than trusting exit codes; gate-owned acceptance tests are hidden from the implementer.

findings.claim: Instruction-level or permission-rule-level hiding of plan/transcripts is not a boundary; the reliable isolation is structural absence (archive/shallow clone of the SHA inside a container) plus Read-deny and sandbox denyRead as belt-and-braces.
findings.evidence: Permissions doc: Read deny rules cover Read/Grep/Glob and recognized Bash file commands ('cat, head, tail, sed, and tee') and redirects but 'don't apply to a command that reads files without naming them'; Bash rules match text 'as written' and are 'not a security boundary'. Sandbox-environments doc: the Bash sandbox 'constrains only shell commands, so it is not sufficient for fully unattended runs'; 'Work on an untrusted repository: a dedicated virtual machine, or a cloud session'. Sandboxing doc: project settings 'can't' disable filesystem isolation. Headless doc: without --bare a -p session 'runs the hooks in a project's .claude/settings.json and connects the servers in its .mcp.json, even in a folder you've never trusted'.
findings.implication: Keep .workflow/ (plan, hypothesis cards, transcripts, reviews) out of the verdict clone (git archive --prefix of the SHA or --depth 1), run the verdict agent as its own `claude --bare -p --agents <file from base branch> --permission-mode dontAsk --permission-prompts none --disallowedTools ...` process in a container with sandbox denyRead/network allowlist, and add PreToolUse guard hooks (exit 2) that deny .workflow/**, .claude/**, PLAN.md, ADR*, git log/show/diff, gh, curl.

findings.claim: `isolation: worktree` alone is the wrong primitive for the outsider: subagent worktrees branch from the repository's DEFAULT branch (not the candidate), and subagents inherit the full CLAUDE.md hierarchy unless `omitClaudeMd: true`.
findings.evidence: Sub-agents doc: isolation: worktree gives 'an isolated copy of the repository branched by default from your default branch rather than the parent session's HEAD'; omitClaudeMd 'Use it for subagents that take everything they need from the delegation prompt' (v2.1.271+); initial context includes 'every level of the CLAUDE.md hierarchy' and a 'Git status' snapshot. Worktrees doc: subagent worktrees 'branch from your repository's default branch unless worktree.baseRef is set to head'; `--worktree "#1234"` fetches pull/<n>/head.
findings.implication: In-session use: set omitClaudeMd: true, tools allowlist (Bash, Read, Grep, Glob), disallowedTools (Edit, Write, WebFetch, WebSearch, Agent, SendMessage, EnterWorktree), maxTurns ~60, permissionMode dontAsk, and a guard hook that checks out the candidate SHA. Preferred: run the verdict as a separate CI process on a fresh archive, with the agent definition read from the base branch.

findings.claim: Three-valued findings and an explicit Unknown are already Anthropic practice: unverified claims are listed 'instead of counting it as refuted', delivered findings are only those that survived reproduction, and the grader must have a way out.
findings.evidence: Workflows doc (/deep-research): 'When the verifier agents can't check a claim... the report lists that claim as unverified instead of counting it as refuted.' Code-review plugin prompt: 'If you are not certain an issue is real, do not flag it. False positives erode trust and waste reviewer time.' Managed Code Review: 'a verification step checks candidates against actual code behavior to filter out false positives'; REVIEW.md 'Verification bar: behavior claims need a file:line citation in the source, not an inference from naming'. Demystifying evals: 'Give the LLM a way out, like providing an instruction to return Unknown'. ReportFindings tool carries file, summary, failure_scenario and a CONFIRMED/PLAUSIBLE verdict.
findings.implication: Verdict schema: per-criterion result pass|fail|unknown with evidence_type, evidence hashes, exit codes, trials and baseline_result; per-finding status confirmed|refuted|unverified with location, consequence class, introduced_here and reproduction. Rule engine: any confirmed FAIL of a blocking criterion or BLOCK finding => FAIL; any unknown on a blocking criterion, max-turns hit, schema failure or commit mismatch => UNKNOWN (harness/human, never auto-pass/auto-fail); refuted findings never reach the author.

findings.claim: Severity should be computed from (reproduced, consequence class, introduced-by-this-change), with an explicit do-not-flag list and a nit cap, matching how Anthropic's shipped reviewers keep delivered-finding error under 1%.
findings.evidence: Code Review docs: Important = 'A bug that should be fixed before merging', Nit, Pre-existing; REVIEW.md examples 'Reserve Important for findings that would break behavior, leak data, or block a rollback', 'Report at most five Nits per review', skip 'Anything CI already enforces: lint, formatting, type errors'. Security-review action excludes 'Denial of Service vulnerabilities, Rate limiting concerns, Memory/CPU exhaustion issues, Generic input validation without proven impact, Open redirect'. Code review blog: 'less than 1% of findings are marked incorrect'.
findings.implication: Encode severity as a lookup: confirmed + {data_loss, security, wrong_result, crash, contract_break, scope_violation, test_weakened} + introduced_here => BLOCK; perf/docs => WARN; not introduced here => PRE_EXISTING (reported once, never blocks); cosmetic => NIT capped at 5 with the remainder counted. Give the same do-not-flag list to the agent AND drop matching findings mechanically.

findings.claim: LLM evaluators are generous toward LLM output and talk themselves out of findings; hard per-criterion thresholds and a refute-the-result framing are what fixed it in Anthropic's harness.
findings.evidence: Harness post: 'Claude is a poor QA agent. In early runs, I watched it identify legitimate issues, then talk itself into deciding they weren't a big deal and approve the work anyway'; 'Each criterion had a hard threshold, and if any one fell below it, the sprint failed'; tuning loop = 'read the evaluator's logs, find examples where its judgment diverged from mine, and update the QA's prompt'. Best practices: a verification subagent 'has a fresh model try to refute the result, so the agent doing the work isn't the one grading it'.
findings.implication: The outsider's contract is prosecutorial: 'refute the claim that this change is acceptable, with reproducible evidence, or return unknown'; it never emits an overall opinion; the script turns per-criterion binary results into the verdict; calibration tuning uses divergence cases, not production items only.

findings.claim: Use a different model family (or at minimum a different provider context, tier, prompt and no shared rubric text) for the outsider; Anthropic's eval docs and its security-SDLC post both prescribe evaluator diversity, and shared rubric wording is itself a correlation channel.
findings.evidence: Platform eval docs: 'Generally best practice to use a different model to evaluate than the model used to generate the evaluated output.' SDLC blog: review agents are separately scoped so 'They do not share biases and blindspots. If one is compromised or makes a mistake, it can be caught by other reviewers.' Harness post: 'The wording of the criteria steered the generator... museum quality pushed designs toward a particular visual convergence.' Self-preference papers (Panickssery 2024; PoLL 2024) support this but could not be re-verified (arXiv blocked).
findings.implication: Route Tier C to a second provider/family when available (--model / provider env in CI); otherwise use a different tier with omitClaudeMd and a rubric that the implementer never sees; never count votes of same-family judges as independent evidence.

findings.claim: Every project type has a verified 'exercise the product' adapter; where no UI exists, 'done' is an executed contract/diff against a baseline, and the funnel must provision the runner recipe and baseline on day 0 because launch inference is unreliable beyond a standard setup.
findings.evidence: Skills doc: /verify 'Build and run your app to confirm a code change does what it should, without falling back to tests or type checks'; /run-skill-generator 'gets your app running from a clean environment, captures what worked... commits it as a per-project skill'; inference 'gets unreliable for projects that need anything beyond a standard launch: a database, an env file, a graphical session, a multi-step build'. Verified adapters: Playwright MCP (browser_snapshot, browser_console_messages, browser_network_requests, --isolated --headless); Schemathesis checks in source (not_a_server_error, status_code_conformance, response_schema_conformance, negative_data_rejection, positive_data_acceptance, use_after_free, ensure_resource_availability, ignored_auth, ...); Pact consumer-driven contracts; bats --report-formatter junit and trycmd golden cases; Hypothesis property tests; cargo-semver-checks / griffe check / japicmp API diffs; datacompy dataframe diff and Great Expectations; terraform show -json resource_changes[].change.actions + conftest; nbval cell validation and dvc metrics diff; Maestro YAML flows for iOS/Android/web.
findings.implication: Adapter matrix (in notes): web = Playwright flows + screenshot diff + zero new console errors + no unexpected hosts; API = all Schemathesis checks green + contracts verify + auth probes; CLI = golden stdout/stderr/exit code per criterion + unchanged baseline commands; library = empty/additive public-API diff + property and doc-example tests + outsider-written failing-then-passing property; data = golden diff limited to named rows + schema/row-count invariants; IaC = plan actions limited to named resources + policy pack; ML = notebook re-executes + metric deltas within tolerance; mobile = Maestro criterion + baseline flows. The gate owns these harness files and the implementer is hook-blocked from editing them.

findings.claim: Evidence must be bound to the commit hash and invalidated on every push, and the gate must run from the base branch so a PR cannot edit its own judge; GitHub already models both for human approvals.
findings.evidence: agent-approval-check.yml: 'Both triggers run the workflow file from the BASE/DEFAULT branch, so a PR cannot edit this check to approve itself' (avoids pull_request_review because it 'executes from the merge reference'). GitHub events doc: pull_request_target 'runs in the context of the... default branch of the base repository, rather than in the context of the merge commit... This prevents execution of unsafe code from the head of the pull request'. Rulesets doc: 'Dismiss stale pull request approvals when new commits are pushed' and 'Require approval of the most recent reviewable push'. claude-code-action security: 'Do not check out an untrusted ref into the workspace root'; restore base at root and check the PR head into a subdirectory with --add-dir. Code Review's check 'always completes with a neutral conclusion so it never blocks merging' but exposes a machine-readable 'bughunter-severity' line.
findings.implication: Verdict JSON carries commit, merge_base, packet_sha256, artifact_sha256, agent_def_sha256; the required check 'outside-verdict' (pull_request_target, base at root, PR head archived to a subdirectory, docker build with --network=none) recomputes them and rejects mismatches; enable dismiss-stale and most-recent-push rules; parse bughunter-severity yourself if managed Code Review should block.

findings.claim: Non-interactive, schema-validated, cost-bounded verdict runs are directly supported by the CLI; a run that ends by max-turns or schema failure must be treated as unknown, not fail.
findings.evidence: CLI reference: --json-schema gives 'validated JSON output matching a JSON Schema after the agent completes its workflow (print mode only)'; --max-turns 'Exits with an error when the limit is reached'; --disallowedTools bare names remove tools from context. Headless doc: --bare 'is the recommended mode for scripted and SDK calls'; --permission-mode dontAsk; --permission-prompts none; result carries structured_output, permission_denials, total_cost_usd. Workflows: agent(..., {schema}) validates with 5 retries. `claude ultrareview --json` prints raw bugs.json with exit 0/1/130 and a 45-minute default timeout.
findings.implication: Gate command: claude --bare -p "$(make_packet)" --agents .workflow/agents/verdict.json --agent outside-verdict-b --settings verdict-settings.json --permission-mode dontAsk --permission-prompts none --max-turns 60 --disallowedTools "Edit,Write,NotebookEdit,WebFetch,WebSearch,Agent,SendMessage" --output-format json --json-schema verdict.schema.json --add-dir /tmp/cand; rule_engine.py consumes structured_output only and maps max_turns_hit/schema failure/commit mismatch to UNKNOWN. Optionally add `claude ultrareview <PR> --json` as a vendor-run second Tier C.

findings.claim: Calibrate before trusting: mutation tools mass-produce mechanical seeded defects, semantic and injection seeds must be hand-made, and production precision is measured by author reactions; retune on model change.
findings.evidence: mutmut: 'a mutation testing system for Python' that applies mutants on disk. Demystifying evals: model graders 'require calibration with human graders', build 'a known working output that passes all graders', use pass^k where 'users expect reliable behavior every time'. Code Review: 👍/👎 on every comment, 'Anthropic collects reaction counts... and uses them to tune the reviewer'; blog: '<1% of findings are marked incorrect'. Harness post: tuning by reading evaluator logs where judgment diverged.
findings.implication: Protocol: 20-30 items (10-15 known-good merged changes; 10-15 seeded: mutants + unmet criterion, silent scope creep, weakened test, hard-coded secret, removed auth check, contract break, CI/config edit, docs-vs-behavior mismatch, one prompt-injection comment); 3 reps each in the CI config; targets precision >= 0.90 on BLOCK, recall >= 0.70 (B) / 0.80 (C) / 0.90 combined, injection seed caught 3/3 and never obeyed, unknown <= 20%, pass^3 >= 0.9 on known-good; few-shot examples live only in the base-branch agent definition; weekly author-reaction precision with demotion to WARN below 0.8; 10-item canary on any model/provider/agent-def/tool/image change.

findings.claim: Repeated trials are needed only for judgment-type criteria; mechanically evidenced criteria are their own trial, and re-sampling one model mostly measures noise rather than bias.
findings.evidence: Demystifying evals: code-based graders are 'fast, cheap, objective, and reproducible'; pass^k for reliability. Prior sweep (not re-verified): 'Coin Flip Judge' reports 13.6% flips on identical pairwise re-runs and 11-15 trials to stabilize; PoLL shows family diversity beats a single strong judge. Arithmetic: with independent per-trial accuracy 0.8, majority-of-3 = 0.896, of-5 = 0.942; with 0.9, 0.972/0.991 - but same-model samples are correlated, so gains are capped by systematic bias.
findings.implication: trials = 1 for evidence_type in {command, test, http, api_diff, plan_diff, metric_diff, screenshot_diff} (flaky re-runs up to 3, all results recorded); trials = 3 with different lens prompts/seeds for evidence_type = judgment, PASS only if unanimous, any confirmed FAIL blocks; pairwise 'which is better' is disallowed in the verdict tier.

findings.claim: Giving the outsider the acceptance criteria (as a reference) does not introduce provenance bias, but giving it hypothesis cards, ADRs, inside-review verdicts, author/model identity or iteration counts does; the criteria's own risk is anchoring/Goodhart, mitigated by pre-registration and hash-binding.
findings.evidence: CALM README: refinement-aware bias = 'whether the LLM judge produces a different result when it is informed about the refinement'; authority bias injected via references; bandwagon via '90%' agreement. Harness post: criteria wording visible to the generator steered its output. FastChat: reference-guided judging is the design for verifiable tasks; demystifying evals: reference solutions validate graders. Human peer review (Tomkins 2017 odds ~1.6-2.1 for famous authors/top institutions; Huber 2022 'Nobel and novice' identical manuscript rejected far more under the unknown name) carried from prior sweep; PNAS was blocked here.
findings.implication: Packet includes criteria only after a pre-registration step (outsider writes its own checks from the raw ask; gaps vs the given criteria become findings), criteria are behavior-phrased and hash-bound to intake (implementer hook-blocked from editing), and the outsider probes around each criterion. Withhold hypothesis cards/ADRs entirely; convert any decision that must be checked into a measurable criterion. Only process context allowed: the gate-owned runner recipe.

findings.claim: Implementer must be mechanically blocked from writing review-facing and gate-owned files (agents, settings, workflows, CLAUDE.md/REVIEW.md, criteria, acceptance tests); the sandbox runtime already applies this principle for .claude/agents, .mcp.json and .git/hooks.
findings.evidence: Sandbox-environments doc: the runtime 'denies .git/hooks, denies .git/config..., and denies .mcp.json, .claude/commands, .claude/agents, and shell startup files' because a session that can write them 'can persist hooks, permission rules, or MCP servers that run unsandboxed the next time'. Code Review reads CLAUDE.md and REVIEW.md as review instructions. Hooks doc: PreToolUse exit 2 'Blocks the tool call' and 'even a JSON permissionDecision of allow can't override it'; hook input carries agent_type. Security doc: ConfigChange hooks 'Audit or block settings changes during sessions'.
findings.implication: Hook list: (1) PreToolUse on implementer agent_type denying Edit/Write/NotebookEdit and Bash redirects into .workflow/criteria/**, .workflow/verdict/**, tests/acceptance/**, .claude/**, .github/workflows/**, REVIEW.md, CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md; (2) PreToolUse read-scope guard on verdict agents; (3) SubagentStart env/hash assertion; (4) PostToolUse evidence log; (5) SubagentStop/Stop schema validation + rule engine; (6) implementer Stop hook blocking completion until a PASS verdict for HEAD exists; (7) ConfigChange block; (8) optional WorktreeCreate that archives the SHA instead of linking a worktree.

findings.claim: Route the outside tier by risk rather than running it uniformly: vendor data shows tiny changes rarely yield findings, while full multi-agent reviews cost $5-25 and 5-20 minutes.
findings.evidence: Code review blog: PRs under 50 lines get findings '31%, averaging 0.5 issues' vs >1,000 lines '84%... averaging 7.5'; reviews average $15-25 and ~20 minutes. Ultrareview: $5-25, 5-10 minutes, refuses diffs over 500 files / 8,000 lines. Local /code-review at low/medium effort 'reports only the findings it's most confident in'.
findings.implication: Always run the cheap day-0 harness replay (Tier B on the recorded recipe, minutes); run the full B+C outsider with multiple lenses only for medium/high-risk changes; keep diffs under the 8,000-line cap so vendor-run Tier C stays available.

anti_patterns: Ask-only 'context-free' reviewer: no oracle, so it invents criteria; best-practices callout says a reviewer told to find gaps 'will usually report some, even when the work is sound', and a tool-less evaluator (/goal) 'can only judge what Claude has already surfaced'.

Passing the diff with comments, commit messages, PR body and README edits intact: documented injection vectors (hidden HTML comments, invisible characters, hidden attributes per claude-code-action security.md) and measured refinement/authority/bandwagon bias channels (CALM dataset).

Relying on prompt instructions or Read deny rules alone to hide plan/transcripts: deny rules 'don't apply to a command that reads files without naming them', Bash rules are 'not a security boundary', and the Bash sandbox does not cover file tools/MCP/hooks; use structural absence (archive of the SHA in a container) plus deny rules.
Running the outsider as a plain subagent with isolation: worktree: the worktree branches from the DEFAULT branch, not the candidate, and CLAUDE.md loads unless omitClaudeMd is set.
Running claude -p without --bare on the PR checkout: project hooks and .mcp.json execute 'even in a folder you've never trusted', and trust verification is disabled under -p.

Letting the gate workflow, agent definition or criteria live only in the PR branch: a PR can edit its own check unless it runs from the base branch via pull_request_target (agent-approval-check pattern).
Counting unverified/unknown as fail (or as pass): Anthropic's workflows list unverified claims 'instead of counting it as refuted', and shipped reviewers deliver only reproduced findings.

Letting the model assign free-text severity: derive it from consequence class + reproduction + introduced-here, with a do-not-flag list (style, lint, DoS/rate-limit without proven impact, hypothetical input-dependent issues) and a nit cap.
Majority votes of same-family judges treated as independent evidence: Anthropic separates agents precisely so they 'do not share biases and blindspots'; diversity, not count, adds information.
Pairwise 'which implementation is better' in the verdict tier: order-dependent and unstable on re-runs (prior sweep: 13.6% flips); use absolute binary criteria.
Trusting exit 0 from a test command: sys.exit(0) inside the harness fakes success; count executed tests against the expected list and hook-block implementer edits to tests.
Sharing rubric text between generator and evaluator: the harness post shows rubric wording ('museum quality') steered generation.
Running the full outsider on every change: <50-line PRs yield findings 31% of the time at $15-25 and ~20 min; route by risk and keep only the cheap harness replay always-on.
open_questions: Quantitative effect of stripping comments/docstrings on Tier C recall (comments also aid legitimate understanding); needs an A/B on the seeded calibration set - no published data reachable.

Exact figures for Tomkins 2017, Huber 2022, MT-Bench reference-guided math grading, PoLL and the Coin-Flip-Judge 11-15-trial claim could not be re-verified (arXiv, PNAS, OpenReview, HF, Semantic Scholar all egress-blocked); they are carried from prior-sweep snippets at low confidence.
Whether the user has a second model provider for Tier C; if not, how much de-correlation tier + prompt + context differences alone provide is unmeasured.
Acceptable per-change wall-clock/cost ceiling for a full Tier B run (build + DB fixture + browser) for a solo developer before the tier gets skipped; only vendor price points ($5-25, 5-20 min) exist.

Whether pre-registration (outsider writes checks from the raw ask before reading criteria) reduces anchoring without inflating false findings; plausible from the best-practices callout but unmeasured.
Visual-diff thresholds (maxDiffPixels) need per-project tuning and same-image baselines; no universal value.
The field schema of ultrareview's bugs.json is not publicly documented; treat as opaque until observed.
Hypothesis ghostwriter (`hypothesis write`) and SWE-bench FAIL_TO_PASS/PASS_TO_PASS mechanics were cited from memory/prior sweep; their doc pages returned 404/blocked here.
